maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO PREVIOUS RULING RESPECTING MOTION TO GO INTO COMMITTEE ON RESOLUTION
REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO PREVIOUS RULING RESPECTING MOTION TO GO INTO COMMITTEE ON RESOLUTION
speechtext:
A matter has arisen as to what was said in the house on Friday. May I refer briefly to the debate which took place on that day. I have no hesitation in saying that, in view of that debate, I am quite concerned about the ruling I made in 1952 with respect to standing order 60.
Hon. members will recall that at that time, after consideration, I gave my views on standing order 60, which reads as follows:
If any motion be made in the house for any public aid or charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof may not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned till such further day as the house thinks fit to appoint; and then it shall be referred to a committee of the whole house, before any resolution or vote of the house do pass thereupon.
From time to time there have been discussions in the house as to whether Mr. Speaker should leave the chair without question put when the motion is called on the second day. A ruling was given by Mr. Speaker Glen a number of years ago, to which I referred in my ruling. Mr. Speaker Glen said, in part, that the debate should be directed to the negative of the motion, and should be general, with no reference to details. I made a similar ruling, in which I concurred in Mr. Speaker Glen's findings, and also ruled that the debate at that time should be directed to the negative of the motion, and should be general.
During the course of the argument, when I intimated that that might be my decision, a number of members reminded me that I would have great difficulty in enforcing it. In fact some hon. members took the attitude: "Either have a full debate or do not have a debate, because otherwise you will not be able to enforce the rules."

Well, I felt I would be able to enforce my ruling and said, at the close of my reasons, that I would ask the co-operation of all hon. members in enabling me to enforce it. I have had the co-operation of all hon. members. But frankly, I must admit that I do not think the decision is workable; I doubt very much if I can enforce that ruling.
On several occasions during the debate on Friday I endeavoured to direct the debate in accordance with what I thought was the proper interpretation of my ruling. However, when I did so I realized that an hon. member could say, "Yes, but I feel this is one reason why Mr. Speaker should not leave the chair", and the hon. member could say, "Therefore I am directing my remarks to the negative."
Also during the debate on Friday the act, which it is proposed by the resolution to continue, was read almost fully into the record. It would have been very difficult for me to have prevented that. If I had said it was an unnecessary detail the answer would have been, "Oh, yes, but that is one reason I think you should not leave the chair; therefore I am directing my remarks to the negative."
There was a very wide debate that day. If hon. members will read Hansard for Friday they will see it was a complete debate on the whole subject of the resolution. Added to that, there was a very long debate on the interpretation of my ruling-and I have no reason to believe that, with a similar resolution, there would not be a similar debate on the interpretation of my ruling.
I think probably we all agreed at that time that the motion for Mr. Speaker to leave the chair was debatable. I now am not sure that we were correct-although we all agreed. The motion, when it is first put, is that at the next sitting of the house Mr. Speaker will leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole on the resolution. That is a decision of the house- that Mr. Speaker will leave the chair at the next sitting.
If the house has reached that decision, then how can the resolution be debatable with the Speaker in the chair when that second day arrives? The house has reached that decision. I think that was a point which was not brought up on previous occasions when this matter was being considered; and it is certainly a point which was not raised on the last occasion.
I am satisfied that the ruling I made in June of 1952 should be revised. When I cannot put it into effect, I do not think I should be asked to let it stand as it is. I

do not think a Speaker should be put in that position. It seems to me it would make for more orderly procedure in the house if, when the motion is called on the second day-that is, the motion that the Speaker do leave the chair-the resolution at that stage were not debated. I am not making a ruling at the present time; I am just expressing a view. It seems to me that no member's rights would be injured in any way. If the Speaker left the chair the resolution would then be before the committee and hon. members could discuss it from every angle with the minister in charge in his seat ready to answer questions and to give necessary information.
I would appreciate it if hon. members would give this matter some consideration. Probably in a few days you will be good enough to give me your views. My only reason for bringing this matter to your attention at the present time is to point out that I have come to the conclusion that I cannot enforce my ruling, that it is not workable or practicable. I think it would be in the interests of the dispatch of business in this house if the Speaker did leave the chair on the second day without question put.
Hon. members may suggest to me that it might be left to the rules committee. I have given that some consideration. This matter has been before three committees at least and no unanimous decision has been arrived at. As Speaker of the House I feel it is my duty to interpret the rules as they are at the present time. If hon. members want to change the rules, then that should be done by the committee; but my task at the present time is to interpret the rules as I see them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is not
much I can add to the previous reply that I gave to my hon. friend on February 4. It is known of course that metals and other materials and equipment of a strategic nature are under export permit control here and have been for a considerable time.
A number of governments are in continuing close association in this work of controlling the movement of such strategic material. These governments agree on the materials to be controlled and the degree of control to be

South Saskatchewan River Project exercised. They have established a system of exchange of documents between importing and exporting countries for assurance to export licensing authorities that goods will reach the destinations indicated. There is a continuing exchange of information on many aspects of the whole problem.
Generally speaking, Canada does not license the export of strategic materials to European destinations unless applications for licences are accompanied by an import certificate issued by the government of the recipient country. This assures that the government of the importing country assumes responsibility for the shipment reaching the declared destination. Further, a verification of delivery is subsequently required in these cases. The greatest care possible, then, is taken with all destinations in assuring that consignees named in export permit applications are acceptable.

The house resumed, from Monday, February 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fournier (Hull) that the house go into committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Wright.

Mr. Speaker, last evening just before the house adjourned I was dealing with the subject of the South Saskatchewan dam and was discussing a private conversation I had had with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) having to do with the dam. I indicated at that time that I tried to suggest to the Prime Minister that all we were interested in as members of parliament was the actual money that it would cost to build the dam. I think I said, but will repeat now, that he reminded me that after all funds would have to be raised for the cost of irrigation and that we 

must give that matter some consideration. I appreciate that point. I shall be a taxpayer for this project to both the federal and provincial governments, as will most, if not all, the people in my constituency.
I realize that the provincial government of Saskatchewan has said that they are prepared to pay their share of the cost of irrigation under the project. Well, I presume that is the case. But at the same time, even if the dam is built, as I hope it will be, there will be no irrigation in the province for some ten years. At that time the present government may still be in office. We will not debate that at the moment. However, whether it is that government or another, if the province of Saskatchewan finds that the load is too heavy for it to carry out. its obligation, then whatever government may be in power provincially may say to the federal government that the load is too heavy for them to carry and that the federal government will have to carry it. I am not saying that will be the case but it could happen.
I do not want to get too far away from the subject, but there are certain projects that have been carried on in Saskatchewan with the help of the federal government, and I should like to refer briefly to our hospitalization scheme. The load is getting very heavy. While the baby was small we in the province of Saskatchewan carried it quite easily, but now that the baby is growing up and getting heavier we in Saskatchewan would like the federal government to assume that responsibility. I hope that that will not be the case when the irrigation project is built.
That is all I am going to say on that point, and I am not going to go into the details of the report of the commission except to say, as I said last night, that reports of commissions do not impress me too greatly. Having said that, however, may I say that I am one of those from Saskatchewan who cannot agree with the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) when he says that the government should gather together all copies of the report of the commission and throw them in the Saskatchewan river. I would agree that when we start to build the dam we should put them at the bottom of it.
It will be a long time before the dam is built.

That may be, but that remains to be seen. In any event, what I am interested in at the moment is not so much what is contained in the various reports. What I am interested in is where we are going from here. If I might be allowed to make a suggestion, I hope it will not be necessary to have any more royal

commissions or commissions. When the Prime Minister spoke last night he put his position before the house. I appreciate his position and I believe most people in the Dominion of Canada and in the house, including members of the opposition, although of course they may not admit it, also appreciate it. Coming to the house on the bus this morning I noticed an item in one corner of the morning Citizen-I did not have one

referring to the South Saskatchewan dam. The reference was to "this big project" and suggesting more study was needed. I am all in favour of more study. In the other corner of the Citizen it said "more investigation".
If more investigation means another commission, then I am absolutely opposed to it, and I want to go on record as saying so. I am going to make a suggestion as to what might be done. Surely we have enough data now as a result of the investigations of the commission and other reports; and let me say that I think their report should be given a good deal of consideration. Some of us do not like the wording of it in certain parts, and in that respect it is like another report with which we were dealing not too long ago. A proper examination and explanation of it indicates that there is some very valuable information provided we use it in a non-political way. Instead of another commission I suggest that we might well have some kind of committee or referee. I would suggest a non-political committee representing all parties in the house.
How do you do that?

The hon. member for Souris says "how do you do that"? It has been done before, and I might add that it has been my experience since coming to the House of Commons that there is much more work done in committees, and in a far less political way, than in this chamber.
Which committee?

Any committees of which I have been a member. I think such a committee could well take a look at the evidence we have. In my opinion there are three things that must be done. The Prime Minister indicated last night that he was not too greatly worried about the cost of the project. I was glad to hear him say that. I am sure he has given that matter some consideration, as all of us must. We must know what kind of isoil there is in the area that is to be irrigated. Surely we do not need to send a commission to Saskatchewan to investigate the soil. We must know the elevation of
South Saskatcheivan River Project the land, and we do not need to send a commission to Saskatchewan to ascertain that. We must also know the rainfall. I am sure that no one would suggest that we should send someone to Saskatchewan to stand outside with a measuring cup for two or three years to find out what the rainfall is. That information is all available in Ottawa. I made it my business to find out from the different departments this morning if this information was available and could be obtained quickly. I was informed that could be done. The committee that I am suggesting might be a small one or a large one. It would have the privilege of calling government officials from the different departments to supply the necessary data. I do not see why we should spend any more money on commissions when we have government officials already on the payroll who can give the information required.
It may also be necessary to obtain the views of the premiers or the ministers of agriculture of the governments of the three prairie provinces. Then let us decide on this matter. I want to say in all sincerity that I hope that another election will not roll around before a decision is made. If it is favourable to us in Saskatchewan, that will be fine. If it is not and if we are going to have to sink, then let us sink with the ship. There is one thing about it. We can only get trimmed once on the issue if a decision is arrived at.
You have been trimmed for years by your government.

That is
what you may think. Speaking yesterday the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) said, if I heard him correctly, that all candidates in the last federal election pledged themselves to the building of the South Saskatchewan dam, or had indicated that in their campaigns. Well, if the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) was never wrong before, he was certainly wrong that time. I was in that last federal campaign and never on any political platform in my constituency was the South Saskatchewan dam mentioned. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) spoke at my convention and it was not mentioned. Another senior minister of cabinet, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), spoke in Estevan and the matter was not mentioned. In all of the campaign carried on in my constituency, and I was at all of the meetings, it was never mentioned.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what will happen in the next campaign I do not know.

South Saskatchewan River Project
You will be running on the Conservative ticket.

I am not
too sure that there will be enough Conservatives in my constituency to elect me and I do not think I could take that chance. However, if this becomes a political football we will have to deal with it then; but I am interested to see that we do not make it a political football at the present time. I wish to say to the government:	Let us
have a decision on this quickly-just as soon as possible. I said last night that I did not think the government could give us a decision right away after the report had become available, but at the same time I would hope that before this house adjourns we will have a decision one way or the other.
I am going to make a plea to the mover of this amendment which may be useless.

We are giving you a
chance.

I will
answer that if you will give me a minute.
The hon. member who moved the amendment to the motion rose in his place and said that he was taking that opportunity to bring this very important subject before the house. He said that it was very dear to his heart and very dear to the hearts of all the people in Saskatchewan. Well, with that there is no dispute. He went on and made what I thought was a very good speech. I pay him the compliment of saying that he made a very good speech and, as a matter of fact, I compliment him on bringing this subject before the house-although the Minister of Agriculture says it could have been brought up in the discussion on his estimates. However, I am with the member for Lake Centre in thinking that we should have had a discussion on this subject as soon as possible-and we have had it. He did not say why he moved his amendment but I presume, and if I am wrong he can correct me, that it was to give other members who were anxious to speak on it, like myself, a chance to speak. Had he not moved the amendment we might have got off on fish, or wheat, or something else and possibly I would not have had an opportunity to speak at this time.
The hon. member went on to say that he was anxious to keep politics out of this, and I am trying to convince myself that was so. I want to say to him:	If he wants to make
it a political issue, what is the hurry; because as far as I know there is no election in the offing at the moment. Why get started on it now? Why play it out now rather than wait? I suggest, as far as timing is

concerned, that it might be better to wait. From a political viewpoint it will have more effect.
From his remarks and actions I take it that the hon. member has no notion of withdrawing his amendment. Before the vote is taken, and while the hon. member has raised a grievance, I will say that I think that moving the amendment has served a good purpose. I am sincere when I say that, but I cannot see any good purpose pressing a vote at this time.
The hon. member and other members have called on the Saskatchewan members to get up and give an independent vote. Someone has suggested that we should press the government for that. I am going to be honest and say that I have not pressed the government for an independent vote on this and I will tell you why. I am satisfied in my own mind at the moment, although I suppose my friends to the left of me will not agree, that if we had an independent vote on this at the present time, regardless of parties to which we belong, the majority of members would not be in favour.
There would be some Liberal members against it.
If my hon. friend would not be so political at the moment we would be able to get somewhere.
Tell us where you are going to run.
There is no difference between the members in the province of Alberta and the province of Manitoba with-
Let us have the vote and find out.

All right, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the hon. member is more interested in the vote than he is in the dam. As soon as this report was received some people suggested: Throw it in the scrap; burn it; throw it in the South Saskatchewan river. Well, that cannot be done. If we had an independent vote, in my opinion, whether the hon. member for Lake Centre agrees with me or not-and I have a right to state my opinion-I do not believe this vote would carry. I have been talking to other members as I have been interested in knowing how some of the Liberals are thinking. I spoke to many of them this morning-they were not from Saskatchewan but from other parts of eastern and western Canada-and they would not like to be called upon at the present

time to get up and make a decision about whether this project should be gone ahead with.
Now, they indicate they are in favour of it. I do not think that a vote serves any good purpose. There is only one good purpose it could serve and that is to bring in politics, which the hon. member from Lake Centre says he is trying to keep out. I am therefore trying to convince myself that is a fact.
My final plea is to ask what good a vote is going to do. Some of the C.C.F. members from Saskatchewan have indicated, for some reason or other, that we are only using this as an excuse for not voting for the amendment or the subamendment. If the hon. member for Lake Centre would take the lead I do not know but I think the other boys would go along and withdraw the subamendment.
A moment ago I think I heard the hon. member for Lake Centre say: Well, we gave you a chance. Let us take a look at that chance. I am not going to admit, Mr. Speaker, that I am any rubber stamp although we have been accused of being rubber stamps and having no independence. I am not going to admit that, but if we just assume it for the moment I would like to say to the hon. member for Lake Centre that two wrongs do not make a right. His amendment serves no purpose other than having a vote at the present time for political purposes. Well, if he wants a vote there will be lots of chance to get a vote and find out just exactly where all members stand later on. I think that he would be doing a great service to the Conservatives left in Saskatchewan if he withdrew the amendment.
The other evening the hon. member said: We want this dam. I will go along with the hon. member for Lake Centre there. We want this dam, but I beg him to keep politics out of it at the present time. If he would do that he would probably make some history in this country. He raised a matter that was very important to himself and all the rest of us in Saskatchewan, and he says that he is trying to keep politics out of it. I do not know whether he would agree with what I have suggested as far as a committee is concerned, but I think he would agree with me that it would be better for us not to have a vote at the present time. I say, and I repeat, that I think that is important at the present time. As far as a vote is concerned, whether it would hurt Liberal members from Saskatchewan or not is, I think, incidental because we either get the dam or we don't and that will be the issue, not how we voted here. If he would
South Saskatchewan River Project follow my suggestion I would be very grateful, and I think it would be helpful.
If I may be allowed to speak for the Conservatives in my constituency, and there were 2,500 in the last federal election, they are very interested in this project for Saskatchewan, and I think they would be very grateful to the only hon. member of their party coming from the province of Saskatchewan if he followed my suggestion. If he does not do so, I am going to have a hard time to convince them, if I should wish to try, that he is not stooping to political manoeuvres. Now, I think that is important.
I wonder if the hon. member could even suggest that.
Pardon?
I do not think that an hon. member should suggest that another hon. member is stooping to political manoeuvres.

History has shown us that things that have happened in the past will, over a period of years, happen again. History has an unfortunate way of repeating itself.
In order to eliminate that situation, and place ourselves in a position where the people of Saskatchewan and the other parts of Canada can look forward to the future with a greater degree of confidence, I should like to lend my assistance to the government and to the people of the Dominion of Canada so that an effort will be made to initiate in the province of Saskatchewan the only method that I know of that can prevent similar conditions occurring in that province. One of the fundamental problems since mankind has been on this earth has been that of dealing with famine. We read in Genesis that at the time of Joseph the land was covered with famine, and that famine was caused by nothing less than a drought. In the year 1516 before Christ it was a problem of the people, and it has been associated with them ever since. In order to eliminate the conditions that existed at that time-they were unaware of what irrigation could do for the people of the world-they used one method, namely, providing in good years for the bad years. In good years they stored up corn for the bad years. The Lord instructed Joseph and they did that during the good years. During the seven good years they stored up sufficient for the seven bad years that were going to be inflicted upon the people, because, as I mentioned before, they had no other solution for their trouble. It is written in Genesis that famine was all over the face of the earth during that period of time. We in this House of Commons must do what lies within our power so that not again in the future at any
South Saskatchewan River Project time, irrespective of what anyone may say about overproduction in this day and age throughout the length and breadth of the land, with the population increasing in the world, shall it be written of us that we contributed to famine in the world.

We read that in the early days the Nile river was used for irrigation purposes so that food could be supplied to the people of that time. During the time of the Roman empire Egypt was the granary of the world. They tried to devise ways and means so that the water would co-operate with the soil to provide the essential of life, which is food. This came to be a continuing problem in the world. We should consider it from that angle if from no other.
Canada is great in the eyes of the world. It has not been too great in its ambition to make provision for the future in connection with irrigation. Last week I checked up on some figures on irrigation in the world and I found that Canada has approximately a million acres under irrigation. The United States, another supposedly advanced country, has 2,200,000 acres under irrigation; Mexico has 5,700,000 acres; Cuba, 50,000 acres; Dominican Republic, 24,000; British Guiana, 100,000; Colombia, 30,000; Peru, 2,400,000; Brazil, 2,200,000; Chile, 3 million; Argentine, 2 million; Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, 8 million; France, 5,700,000; Italy, 4,920,000; Spain, 3,740,000; Morocco, 1,500,000; Algeria, 400,000; Greece, 600,000; Syria, 620,000; Hungary, 40,000; Lebanon, 74,000; Pakistan, 30 million. It was only a few years ago that we had its Prime Minister in our country. China has 47,500,000 acres under irrigation; Japan, 7,600,000; Thailand, 1,800,000; the Philippines, 1,120,000; India, 35 million; Ceylon, 400,000; Indo-China, 1 million; Java, 8 million; Australia, 2,700,000; New Zealand, 250,000, making a total of approximately 180 million acres of land of the world under irrigation. Without these 180 million acres of land under irrigation famine would stalk the face of the earth. Therefore I submit, Mr. Speaker, that irrigation is a good prospect. Wherever irrigation has been instituted it has neither been abandoned on any large scale nor reduced to any great extent in any country of the world. In any country where there is water and suitable land, if they are not brought together it is wastage of the soil and it is wastage of lives, because production on that soil results in giving people the opportunity to live somewhere in the world.

Since we have learned it let us adapt ourselves to it and unite our experience with the experience of people throughout the whole world, and utilize the waters that flow that were given to us for that purpose as well as for other purposes. Water has been utilized since the beginning of time for that purpose and will be utilized for that purpose until the end of time. Our only solution in the southwest area is water. There is no other solution. The practice of summer fallowing was initiated and has been continued over the years. The cost, year after year, of letting all that land remain idle has been so great that, as I have said, it would build a dozen South Saskatchewan river projects.

That is what P.F.R.A. was initiated to do- to have that land brought into operation, and to eliminate the conditions which made it impossible to bring the area to a point where it could make its contribution to the national life of the country. And does anyone think that we will not have periods of drought again? Does anyone think we can stand idly by after suffering from drought over the years, without giving the people of the southwest any evidence that preparations are being made on the part of the government in respect of what it will do in years to come? I would not be a party to any policy or support any government that takes the position that it will not utilize what has been shown necessary by evidence through the years, or that will not accord the people their rights. Since the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Studer) has spoken, I am even more timid because I am a member of the legal profession. However, he did mention that sometimes we are able to get people out of trouble, and perhaps I can suggest something that may be of some use to the people from western Canada. It has been my observation generally that property and civil rights, such as are involved in this case, are always under the legislative jurisdiction of the provinces, and in my own province of Ontario these matters are usually looked after by the province. I should like to suggest that so far as Saskatchewan is concerned the province has a legitimate claim. First of all, when the province was formed, which as I remember was some time around 1905, the resources were reserved to the federal government and were not returned to the province until many years later.
During that period much of the immigration to and settlement of the now arid area of southern Saskatchewan took place, and the federal government, both parties at one time or another, had the control of it. Therefore I suggest that the federal government, having been in a sense responsible for that settlement, owes a duty to Saskatchewan by reason of the improper, inefficient or unknowledgeable administration during that period. I would suggest that their duty is to try to remedy the defect, to try to remedy what took place. One obvious remedy would be to remove these people and place them elsewhere, but such a remedy is never simple of accomplishment. If another remedy is to provide irrigation to permit the land on which these people were settled to become properly arable, then I would suggest that is a suitable solution.
The report of the commission has been made and it indicates to a certain extent anyway that the project may not be economically sound. In that event, since I believe that the federal government has a duty to the province of Saskatchewan, I would suggest that the government study earnestly what can be done in the way of irrigation It may be that the P.F.R.A. engineers have a proper solution or it may be that they have not. Nevertheless I suggest that in fairness to the province of Saskatchewan-and I think this feeling is held generally by those in
South Saskatchewan River Project Ontario-a proper study should be made reasonably quickly. The information is now available, and a decision should be made as to what should be done so far as irrigation is concerned.
I do not think any person from Ontario feels, as some of the Saskatchewan members sometimes suggest, that Saskatchewan is something that is outside the pale. Nor do we ever feel that we do not need Saskatchewan. We regard it as a most valuable part of our national economy, and obviously it is only by the complete integration of all natural resources in the total economy of Canada that we can achieve the greatness which is necessary to this country. When people from Saskatchewan make comments about the rather indifferent attitude of those from the east I think they are sometimes expressing opinions in which they do not really believe. It would be silly for any hon. member of this house to try to write off Saskatchewan or any other province and suggest that when something is due to them they should not receive it. Therefore, acknowledging that we possibly owe a debt to Saskatchewan, my only suggestion is that a study be made of the problem as soon as possible using the large amount of information available, and that a solution be reached and action be taken.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks following what has been said by the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) and the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter). First of all I am not a lawyer, and that may be of some help to me here. But I do want the people of Saskatchewan to know, and especially members of this house from Saskatchewan, that we in Ontario are right behind them as far as we can go. I do not think there is any doubt about that. That feeling is not the monopoly of a couple of Conservative members. It is held equally by every Liberal member of the house from eastern Canada. We are most sympathetic to their cause.
At this point I should like to pay a tribute to the wonderful sales effort put on by Liberal members from Saskatchewan in connection with this project. They have visited our offices, they have talked to us on every and all occasions on which we have come in contact with them. They have tried to explain the difficulties they have had and the necessity of something being done. I pay tribute to their work and I want to let their constituents know what wonderful work they have done and are doing on their behalf. There is no monopoly there as far as the Conservatives

South Saskatchewan River Project are concerned-or the other parties. The Liberals from Saskatchewan have done a wonderful job.
Going further, I must say I admired the attitude the Prime Minister has taken about this, in comparison with the attitude of the other parties concerned. It was one of responsibility-responsibility that has been evident in his actions since he has been our Prime Minister. I say to the people of Canada and of this house in particular, Mr. Speaker, thank God we have a Prime Minister and a cabinet who must be convinced of the right way before they will go ahead and spend $2 million, $84 million, $350 million or whatever it may be. They must be convinced they have the answer before they will go ahead on any project, be it this one or be it any other. They will not be pressured into building the South Saskatchewan dam or anything else until they are convinced it is right to go ahead, to take the taxpayers' money and go ahead with that or any other project. Thank heaven we have that cabinet and that Prime Minister with us.

I just want a minute of the time of the house because I too have been visited by the Liberal members from Saskatchewan who have taken my time and their time to explain and re-explain to me the South Saskatchewan project and its benefits. Perhaps the views of a member who is not elder but who has grey hairs would be useful.
We should let the people of western Canada know that we in eastern Canada want to be helpful. We have long ago realized, if we have not expressed the view, that we in eastern Canada can be neither healthy nor prosperous without western Canada; that we appreciate that the metropolis of Winnipeg, and Regina in the heart of the wheat belt, and the great city of Vancouver, which has a twelve-months port, are dependent on the wheat belt.
As I understand it, and as simply as I can put it, we are trying to build a lake in the centre of the prairie provinces. In eastern Canada we have much water. We have too much water at times but you in western Canada lack water. We cannot bring you our water; there is no way of doing that; there is no way of our sharing it with you. But we can share our wealth with you in order that wealth may provide water for you.
We in eastern Canada look upon the South Saskatchewan project as being in the interests of all the people of Canada and not of any particular part of it. As for myself, I was very disappointed that some doubt was cast upon this scheme, but it has been; and that 

is something that you people from Saskatchewan will have to overcome in some way. Remove the doubt; that is your immediate task.
Much more progress can be made if all of us in this house would devote ourselves to removing as quickly as possible that doubt which has been cast upon the project by the report. I assure the members from western Canada that we shall support the project willingly and anxiously.

Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of speaking on this matter but after hearing the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), and the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Studer), whom we heard a while ago, I thought I might add my contribution.
We know that these gentlemen who are from Saskatchewan are very anxious to have this dam built and we also know that, as a member said a moment ago, Canada can only be prosperous provided the whole country is prosperous. If all of the provinces are not prosperous Canada cannot be prosperous.
I am sure that we have great admiration for the people of the west who have done a wonderful job in building that part of this country. We have great admiration for those men who have fought the battle to have this dam built. But if we stop to think for a moment, we will all agree that up to now Almighty God seems to have been pretty good to the people of Saskatchewan. The farmers seem to be getting their fair share of prosperity and we are glad they are getting that fair share of prosperity because they deserve it. We hope they will continue to be prosperous for many years so that we may enjoy that prosperity with them.
The government, however, has a duty to perform which cannot be limited to any one section of this vast country, nor to any one province. It is the duty of the government to find out and investigate closely just where and how money received from the taxpayers can be spent most judiciously. It may be all right for the members from Saskatchewan to concentrate all their efforts on forcing the government to act immediately on this dam. I have already said before that I admire them for that, because if they can get this dam for their province it will no doubt add to the great prosperity of Saskatchewan and, eventually, of Canada. We would all benefit from that. But, Mr. Speaker, the government must, before spending the taxpayers' money, look forward and see what the best results can be for the country as a whole. Until it has investigated every means of irrigation I

think it would be foolish at the present time for the government to endeavour to build this dam until it has further information. I base my views on the report of the commission. Some people have said-
That is not the Currie report you have, is it?

-that the commission should not have gone into all these things. To me, however, the commission was a commission duly appointed by this government and I am sure that its members endeavoured to do their duty as they saw fit. They have had expert advice and they are looking to the prosperity of Canada as much as we are.
I would refer to page 6, "Findings and Recommendations":
1.	The commission finds that at present the economic returns to the Canadian people on the investment in the proposed South Saskatchewan river project (central Saskatchewan development) are not commensurate with the cost thereof; though the project would yield social returns which, while they cannot be measured for the purpose of this report, would be of great value to the region in which it is situated.
2.	The commission recommends that, when the time comes that the project represents the then best use of water for irrigation, the present finding should be reviewed in the light of changing conditions . . .
3.	The commission finds that the available data, which are by no means complete, indicate that the said project does not represent the most profitable and desirable use which can be made of the physical resources involved . . .
5. The commission finds that the future demand for water for irrigation could be such as to exhaust the available flow of the South Saskatchewan river, and recommends, therefore, that without delay a comprehensive, long-range program be developed that would result, over the years, in the most beneficial use being made in the interests of the people of Canada of the waters of the Saskatchewan river from its head waters to the sea.
I therefore concur entirely with the remarks made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on Monday evening when he said, as reported on page 1770 of Hansard:
The government is not prepared to go ahead, without further information, to recommend to parliament the expenditure of the amounts estimated by the commissioners, and will not take it upon itself to do that until it has further information . . .
The further information is as to whether or not this is the best use to be made of that great national asset. Personally I think that it is a good use to be made of it, and if I can be convinced to the extent where I can honestly say that I believe it to be the best I will recommend to my colleagues to make the recommendation to parliament. But I want to be sure that if this asset is used in this way it will not be apparent shortly afterward that there was a better use to which it should have been put.
As a businessman, Mr. Speaker, I say this is not the proper time to go ahead with this project because the commission has stated that there might be other plans in the
South Saskatchewan River Project future that would be cheaper. Since we have to spend the taxpayers' money judiciously, I think it would be a good idea to have further investigation. If we find at a later date that this is a bona fide project, then we could go ahead with it. I would then be entirely in favour of that project.
I heard an hon. member state a few minutes ago that he had never been asked to vote in any particular way. I can say that since I have been in this house-it is only a short time-no one has ever asked me to vote in any particular way or told me to do anything I did not want to do. I should like to tell the gentlemen who have spoken, and who have told us that we have to vote in a certain way, that I shall vote with the government because I am convinced that the government is right. I am proud of the words used by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) the other night. Like a good father with a family of ten children, he wants to see that the money the government is spending is spent fairly and for the good of the whole of Canada. It is for that reason that I shall vote with the government, because I am convinced that the Prime Minister has the welfare of Canada at heart and it is for that reason he is delaying this project. He is not sure that it is the best way to spend the taxpayers' money.

I did not
intend to take part in this debate, but after hearing the remarks of the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Studer), I believe I would be remiss in my duty as a member of the New Brunswick bar if, at this stage, I did not take up the cudgels and say a few good words on behalf of the lawyer members of the government and the House of Commons. The hon. member suggested, when speaking on this amendment, that the house should be divided into three sections, and that the lawyers should occupy the limbo section. If we were to follow the pattern set out by the hon. member and had one section which was not very interesting, then a heavenly section, a purgatory section and then limbo, in what section would the hon. member for Maple Creek like to see himself?
There have been many things, mostly bad, said about lawyers throughout the ages. One definition which has always struck me as being very much to the point, Mr. Speaker, was coined by a great British jurist when he said that lawyers were comparable to a pair of shears in that they cut everything that comes between them but they never nick one another. May I remind the hon. member that all these unfriendly, uncharitable, sometimes witty but often "corny"-to use a modern expression-darts which have been thrown at us have always been blunted on

South Saskatchewan River Project the Canadian lawyers' armour of professional solidarity and dignity. We are strengthened in the realization that most of those who criticize us most, severely deserve nothing but the divinely inspired words:
"Father forgive them; they know not what they do."
Before resuming my seat, may I ask the hon. member for Maple Creek where he would find a cabinet in his government today were it not for the thirteen able lawyers who make a good part of the 20-member cabinet of the present government?

They are good
lawyers.
I said that.

I should like to say a few words on this subject because the real roots of my very existence stretch down into the dry, droughty soil of Saskatchewan. I recollect quite vividly what the lack of rainfall meant to many people in Saskatchewan. I should like to say also that, coming from the province of British Columbia, no tirade of abuse has ever been levelled at me because I voted in support of additional payments to the people of Saskatchewan for grain. Further than that, I should like to say that we are representatives of Canada, and not just representatives of one constituency in the dominion. I feel, therefore, that on this occasion it is necessary to speak about unity in Canada. I am not going to devote one instant while I am on my feet to speaking about the merits or demerits of the South Saskatchewan development. The whole carcass, if I may use that expression, of the subject has been gnawed over in this house for a couple of days. I do not think anything I could say with respect to that carcass would be edifying to any member of the house.
I should like hon. members to allow their minds to go back to the days of Upper and Lower Canada to see what great advancement the Canadian nation has made in unity, not provincial unity, not parochial unity, but in national unity for the general welfare of the Canadian people. It is that point about which I am most concerned. In that connection, sir, may I say that some of our great prime ministers of the past, the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the late Right Hon. R. L. Borden, the late Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, and our present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) have added tremendously to the national unity of Canada, compared to what it was at the turn of this century. Therefore, sir, rather than delay the house unduly in connection with what I consider to be a proper appraisal of national unity, I should like to quote a citation from

the life of Lord Rosebery as written by Lord Crewe. Before I do that may I say that there are certain phrases in the quotation I shall read that deal with Scottish union as they apply to the United Kingdom and also unity within the United Kingdom, and wherever the phrase occurs in what I am about to quote we can substitute the word "confederation" or "confederacy" as it applies to the Dominion of Canada. I should like to put on record the words of Lord Rosebery with respect to unity as they appear on page 49 of this volume. As this quotation was applicable in his day, so also is it applicable today in Canada:
Our ancestors put their hands to a mighty work, and it prospered. They welded two great nations into one great empire, and moulded local jealousies into a common patriotism. On such an achievement we must gaze with awe and astonishment, the means were so adverse and the result so surprising. But we should look on it also with emulous eyes. Great as that union was, a greater still remains. We have in our generation, if we would remain a generation, to effect that union of classes without which power is a phantom and freedom a farce. In these days the rich man and the poor gaze at each other across no impassable gulf; for neither is there in this world an Abraham's bosom of calm beatitude. A powerless monarchy, an isolated aristocracy, an intelligent and aspiring people, do not together form the conditions of constitutional stability. We have to restore a common pulse, a healthy beat to the heart of the commonwealth. It is a great work, the work of individuals as much as of statesmen, . . .
I should like hon. members to pay particular attention to this phrase. I continue:
. . . alien from none of us, rather pertinent to us all; each in his place can further it. Each one of us-merchant and clerk, master and servant, landlord and tenant, capitalist and artisan, minister and parishioner-we are all privileged to have a hand in this most sublime work of all; to restore or create harmony betwixt man and man; to look, not for the differences which chance or necessity has placed between class and class, but for the common sympathies which underlie and connect all humanity. It is not monarchs, or even statesmen, that give to a country prosperity and power. France in 1789 had a virtuous monarch and able statesmen. But the different classes of the community had then become completely estranged, and the upper crust of society was shivered to dust by the volcano beneath. In this country the artificial barriers which separate class from class are high enough, but, thank God, they are not insuperable. Let us one and all prevent their becoming so. A great page records the bloodless and prosperous history of the Scottish union. A greater page lies vacant before us on which to inscribe a fairer union still."
That is the crux of my remarks, Mr. Speaker. As Canadians, let us determine to continue the great work of bringing about a greater national harmony in the Dominion of Canada. That has been exemplified by other members here this afternoon, one from the maritimes and also from Ontario and Quebec. Let us agree that if the economics

of this project are such that they warrant the expenditure of the amount of money called for either by the commission report or in the estimates of the cost by the federal government, we shall see to it that through our voice in this parliament we shall bring about, as the closing words of the quotation I have just given say, a greater and more lasting harmony and unity than we have had.

subtopic: MERCANTILE BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
It will be a pleasure to say a few words on this bill to incorporate the Mercantile Bank of Canada. The incorporators are five well-known gentlemen, three of whom are extremely well known to Canadians. The first is Mr. J. B. Carswell of Vancouver, who during the war was director general of the department of munitions and supplies in Washington. He of course is a well known consulting engineer and at the present time has considerable to do with the Kitimat construction and other big projects in British Columbia. Mr. Arthur Cross is also one of the Canadian incorporators, and he was a senior partner of P. S. Ross and Sons of Montreal, chartered accountants. He is a past president of the Dominion Steel and


Coal Corporation and a past director of the Royal Bank of Canada. Senator Bouffard is of course well known to most of us. Aside from being a lawyer, he is president of La Banque d'Economie de Quebec, Quebec city.
Then we have the last two directors, C. J. Endert and H. E. Moquette, both of whom are managing directors of the Dutch bank, Nationale Handelsbank N.V. of Amsterdam, Holland. The capital is $3 million divided into 300,000 shares of the value of $10 per share. I understand $1,500,000 will be subscribed if the House of Commons allows this bill to go through. The head office is proposed for the city of Montreal, and as soon as possible thereafter a branch will be opened in the city of Vancouver because one of the purposes of this incorporation is to supplement the international trading services of the existing banking system of Canada. This charter, as hon. members will see from section 5 of the bill, if passed and accepted by the house will continue in force, as will the charters of all other banks of Canada, until the decennial revision, namely July 1, 1954.
I am prepared to give further details but the bill has been considered in the other place, has been given third reading and passed. I suggest that it should be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce where we are prepared to give any and all explanations, to call any witnesses that the members may desire, to expose the plans and the necessity, purpose and reasons for the passing of the bill and the application in further detail.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce.

Mr. Speaker, the main amendment was moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) in the following terms:
This house regrets that in the estimates presented to this house no provision has been made for immediately proceeding with the construction of the South Saskatchewan river dam.
When the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) began his speech yesterday he attempted to convince hon. members that the very small item now in the estimates for further surveys in relation to this project is an item that in fact could be used for the construction of the project. The minister went to great lengths to attempt to show the house that this vote could be used for construction. He even went so far as to say that somebody had made a mistake, that the vote should have been $1 million instead of $500,000 as appears in the estimates.
I have seen the government make a lot of mistakes during this session, but I do not imagine the treasury board let half a million dollars go by without realizing it. I noticed that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) did not say that the item of $500,000 in the estimates should have been $1 million. It is a case once again of the Minister of Agriculture attempting to say in another way that the people of Saskatchewan can still expect that the project will be completed.
A lot has been said in this debate about members of parliament having a free vote.
South Saskatchewan River Project We have heard the hon. member for Outre-mont-St. Jean (Mr. Bourque) and the hon. member for Durham (Mr. James) get up and say that votes are always free, that there is never any pressure put on Liberal members-
On a point of order, I do not believe that the hon. member for Durham ever said any such thing.
Oh, I am sorry; that is correct.
Although I would agree with it heartily.

It was the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart). The hon. member for Durham agrees, so we have three of them saying the same thing. That being the case, I suggest that members on the government side of the house from the province of Saskatchewan have no choice, if they really want the South Saskatchewan dam built, and should say not only by voice, which is important, but by vote, which in my opinion is of equal importance, that the project should be gone ahead with. The hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Studer) said: Well, in this place it does not matter how you vote; it only matters how you talk. I wonder how the member for Maple Creek got his seat in the House of Commons. Was it by the way the people in his constituency talked or was it by the way they voted?
Speaking in the House of Commons is important in that we can bring issues to the attention of members, and we can plead that members should support certain issues. The vote is of extreme importance and any vote which has been taken against the amendment asking that the dam should be built is, in my opinion, a very distinct disservice to the people of Saskatchewan who are anxious that this project be gone ahead with.
I have been saying that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is attempting to dangle a carrot on a stick before the people of Saskatchewan in the coming election. He is trying to keep the door open and to say that perhaps that small item in the estimates may be sufficient to start construction of the project. Well, it is a carrot on a stick, but the carrot is getting smaller as the years go by. I notice that the estimates for this project for the year 1949-50, in other words the 1949 election year, were $2 million. The estimates for 1950-51 were divided into two categories. Both estimates that might have been used for this project and were used no doubt for certain surveys on the project totalled $1,775,000. The next year's estimates were again reduced, to $1,545,000. The 1952-53 estimates for this project were once again reduced, being down to $1,245,000. The

South Saskatchewan River Project 1953-54 estimates that were recently tabled for this project total only $636,438.
We had a $2 million estimate in 1949-50, the last federal election year, and this year, another federal election year, the estimate is one-third of that $2 million. That estimate, taken in conjunction with the royal commission's adverse report, together with the stand taken by our own Saskatchewan Liberal members, suggests to me that the chance of getting the dam now is just about one-third the chance we had in 1949-50.
Well, the Minister of Agriculture was attempting to keep the door open, attempting to say there is a little item in the estimates and that there might be a little hope yet for the project. I notice that he said there was no division in the cabinet-there should not be, either-and so when the Prime Minister stated the cabinet's position we got the record straight. The Prime Minister said at page 1770 of Hansard:
The government is not prepared to go ahead, without further information, to recommend to parliament the expenditure of the amounts estimated by the commissioners, and will not take it upon itself to do that until it has further information.
The Minister of Agriculture says the door may still be open. The Prime Minister says the government is not prepared to go ahead. We have had members from Saskatchewan saying they could not vote in favour of the dam at this time, in favour of the amendment or the subamendment, because such a vote might defeat the government. They would not want to do 'anything that would defeat the government. Apparently if they have a choice between supporting this government, with its colossal majority, adding one more vote to a very large and unessential majority in any given vote, they prefer to do that rather than to vote for a project that is essential to their constituents and to the people of Saskatchewan.
We were not asking any of them to do anything that would vote the government out of office; though mind you, I imagine we will be leaving here in a few weeks and will be out fighting a federal election. It does not matter at all to me; in fact it would be just fine if the election were called now and we could get out a little bit sooner. That has nothing to do with their proposition. They would not vote for it because it might defeat the government and they would not want to do that.

Order. I am not entirely convinced that the hon. member has the right to speak again at this time. Citation 293 of Beauchesne's third edition reads as follows:
After an amendment has been moved and seconded, the question on the amendment is pro-


posed, and any member who speaks after that question has been proposed speaks to it and not to the main question. When the amendment has been disposed of and the main question is again proposed, any member can speak who has not already spoken on the main question, whether he spoke on the amendment or not.
I would ask hon. members to notice carefully the following words:
The mover and seconder of the amendment having spoken to the main question cannot speak again to it. The same rule applies, of course, to the case of an amendment to an amendment.
The original amendment to the main motion was moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and seconded by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). The subamendment was moved by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) and seconded by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). Is not then the hon. member for Assiniboia prevented from speaking to the main amendment? Unless any hon. members have arguments to the contrary I am afraid that I shall have to rule accordingly.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to try to argue to the contrary but I would like to point out two things. The first is that the citation you have just read from is not from any standing order. It is one of those many citations and precedents which I sometimes think cause us more trouble than they do us good. The other point I would draw to Your Honour's attention is that although those words have been there in that paragraph for all these years I have never known them to be applied. Time and again seconders of amendments and seconders of subamendments have been permitted to speak at the succeeding stage of the debate.
I would suggest that we should hardly be changing a practice that has been followed down through the years, particularly when the suggestion to do so is on the basis not of a standing order but of a paragraph known as a citation tucked away in the book.
Of course, there are many citations in Beauchesne-
Hear, hear.

-to the effect that if an hon. member moves an amendment or, having seconded an amendment, speaks to the amendment he is then prevented from speaking on the main motion. I think I would have to apply the same ruling to a subamendment. I am afraid I will have to rule that the hon. member for Assiniboia has not the right to speak at this time.
Mr. Speaker-
Is it on a point of order?

On a point of order. I am not an expert on the rules but in that respect I find myself very much at home with the great percentage of members in the house. However, I do think that there must be some common sense applied to a matter of this kind. If I may, I should like to bring what I believe is an element of common sense to this decision. It seems to me that when there is a main motion before the house, then the house membership has a right, while that motion is before the house, to speak. There is no doubt about that, and no one will deny that position. When an amendment is introduced I should think no one would object to anyone in the house speaking whether or not he has spoken before, because when an amendment is introduced a new subject is injected into the debate. For this reason the membership of the house has a right to discuss it and state their point of view.
Then when a subamendment is introduced, surely the same thing applies. Another new subject has been injected into the debate, and surely no one will suggest that the house membership has not the right to speak on that subamendment. Those three divisions having been properly established, then surely the reverse applies. After all, because a member does not speak at one of these stages surely he is not denied the right to speak when that stage is again reached by the house. I am not referring to a question of rules or anything technical, but I believe if you think this over, Mr. Speaker, you will see there is some injustice done if that common sense approach is denied to the membership of the house. I leave that to you, because your acknowledged fairness in matters of this kind will take that point into consideration. If a member has a right to speak at some stage of the debate, surely he has not denied himself that right by not having participated at that time.

speechtext:
Just to complete the picture, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I was most interested in the argument of the hon. gentleman. What is the main motion before the house? It is that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of supply. That is one stage where any member can speak, move an amendment or a subamendment. No one ever discusses the main motion that Mr. Speaker do or do not leave the chair. Usually they add some regret or ask some redress.
When the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) spoke, he spoke about the South Saskatchewan matter. In his amendment he blamed the government for not proceeding immediately with these works. His amendment was seconded by the Leader of
South Saskatchewan River Project the Opposition (Mr. Drew). Later on the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) moved the subamendment, and if I recall correctly the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) seconded the subamendment. In his speech he covered the whole amendment and the subamendment, and to my knowledge he did not forget anything.
Do you not think, Mr. Speaker, that this citation has some good foundation? If you want to follow the other citation that says speeches should not be repetitious, I am sure all this will be a repetition of things that have been said many times. In the interests of orderly discussion in the house, once we have said everything we have to say, repetition cannot help our case.
