speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I thought we were discussing the South Saskatchewan project or development. Perhaps 1 am mistaken and do not know enough about it. That is what has been discussed for two days. The hon. gentleman is now repeating himself because Mr. Speaker let him go on a second time and speak on the amendment. I would not apply the rule too strictly, but in the name of common sense 1 think we have discussed this at length and repetition would not enlighten the members of parliament or the public.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I am certainly not an authority on the rules. In my experience in this house, I have never seen Your Honour rule a member out of order because he may have spoken on the subamendment and then wished to speak on the main amendment.

I quite agree with the hon. gentleman in that statement, but the difficulty in which I find myself is that the hon. member for Assiniboia seconded the subamendment. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) has raised a very interesting question, and I am inclined to agree with his viewpoint. 1 gather from what he said that hon. members who had not spoken on the main amendment should now have the

South Saskatchewan River Project opportunity of doing so. I agree with him. That is in accordance with the rules of the house, as he has stated.
However, the rule also is to the effect that an hon. member who moves or seconds a subamendment and speaks, not only speaks to the subamendment but also speaks to the amendment.
In the latter part of citation 293,1 find these words:
The mover and seconder of the amendment having spoken to the main question cannot speak again to it. The same rule applies, of course, to the case of an amendment to an amendment.
My ruling is that the hon. member for Assiniboia, having seconded the subamendment and having spoken to the subamendment, is prevented from speaking to the amendment. This does not, however, prevent other hon. members who have not spoken to the amendment from speaking to the amendment at this time. The hon. members who moved and seconded the subamendment along with the hon. member who moved the main amendment cannot speak at this time.

would ordinarily hesitate a long time, Mr. Speaker, before entering a debate which might more properly be had on the occasion of the budget or at some other time. However, I think possibly I can make some slight contribution to this debate, and that is why I rise at this time.
I come from our most westerly province, and I think I will be understood when I say that we and the three western provinces enjoy something of a community of interest. I should like to think that all the people in British Columbia would be as anxious to see this project go ahead as are the people of Alberta and Saskatchewan. This is one of the great national projects upon which this government has embarked; and I think the great national projects upon which we have embarked constitute probably the finest contribution of this twenty-first parliament. It would be a fortunate circumstance if these projects could be by climatic and economic necessity spread equally all across this country, because a project of this size, or a project of the size of the St. Lawrence seaway, must be of benefit to all Canada as well as to the area in which they stand.
In connection with this amendment I am deeply concerned about the reported remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) when he was recently in the west, and I am equally concerned about statements made by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue).

As far as I can see they take the stand: costs be hanged; let us build it anyway.
We have had members on the other side of the house endeavour to embarrass the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) by suggesting that he is now tarrying over a thing which his people want immediately.
You cannot embarrass him.

Well, probably it is a good thing for Canada that he cannot be embarrassed. I would say this, that if he is embarrassed in his own province of Saskatchewan-and I do not think he is, very much-I should like to think that the taxpayers in the other provinces of Canada would thank him and the government for having the moral courage to take the position they did.
Irrigation farming, I have learned after considerable study, is the most hazardous of all types of farming. I know some of the history of irrigation in the areas represented by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Wylie) and the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore). It is a type of agriculture that, after the water is available, involves a very great cost in preparing the land for the irrigation. I have seen in that area those big land planes, as they call them, in which the land has to be shaved down to make a gradual slope so the water can be economically used. When the water is put in this particular area of Saskatchewan, as undoubtedly it will be some day, you are going to revolutionize Saskatchewan to this extent, that you are going to cease having the monoculture that is at present practised there. I am of the opinion that as soon as the water is put on the land, that land will have a value of $150 to $200 an acre. Farm production is dependent upon soil resources, sunshine and water. On the prairies today two of these essentials are under control. The third is not under control. The proposal to bring irrigation to that area is to bring the third essential under control.
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) said that Saskatchewan was a grain-growing province. I do not believe grain would continue to be the primary product grown on that irrigated land. I do not for a minute believe that. They would immediately have to get into, on account of the cost value of the land, the specialized crops for which Alberta is making a great name for itself today.
In our province of British Columbia we have a situation not dissimilar to that projected in the South Saskatchewan scheme. We have areas where the water has to be raised to the benchlands in our Okanagan for

the production of fruit. The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones) will bear me out when I say that in that area the gross production from some of that land-I mean gross production to the farmer-is of the nature of $2,000 an acre; yet they find that the maximum limit to which they can raise water effectively is something under 200 feet. That is something that should induce us not to cast aside advice but to use all the advice that we can possibly obtain.
The P.F.R.A. engineers in Saskatchewan, and indeed in all the prairie provinces, have in recent years done a magnificent job on soil and water conservation on relatively smaller projects. This is a very large project. I have no doubt that for years the P.F.R.A. engineers had been thinking in terms of this larger project; but I am equally convinced that they have not given the thorough study and inspection to the costs which would warrant the approval of the government of the scheme as a whole.
The government employed a commission. Two of these men I do not know, but I remember reading the late Dr. Widtsoe's writings fifteen years ago. I am informed that he was the best irrigation engineer on this continent, which might make him one of the better irrigation engineers of the world. The commission made a suggestion that the cost was excessively high. When I go to a doctor and he tells me something I do not like to hear I do not say, "Off with his head." They are doing that in Russia today, but I hope we will not do it in Canada. I think we have arrived at a position where we need additional information. Surely this project is of sufficient size to warrant all the information we can collect.
We are not an overly cautious people, and I would not be too cautious in this regard, but I do not want to be like the Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Lake Centre or the hon. member for Assiniboia, and throw all caution to the winds; because the effect of this amendment is that regardless of cost we shall build it anyway.
As a taxpayer in another province I have said that we in British Columbia are just as interested in the building of that dam and the bringing of irrigation to the province of Saskatchewan as the people of that province, and we want to see it. We were as cruelly disappointed by the findings in this report as were the people of Saskatchewan, but at the same time to take the stand that regardless of cost we must proceed at once is to take a stand that I do not think should
South Saskatchewan River Project be shared by the people of any of the provinces, including Saskatchewan, and that is why I propose to vote against the amendment.

I do not
pose as an authority on the constitution, but to my knowledge there are three qualities a government must have to stay in office. It must be able to carry the speech from the throne; it must be able to carry its budget, and it must be able to go into supply in order to vote money. At page 1591 of Hansard the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) moved:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that in the estimates presented to this house no provision has been made for immediately proceeding with the construction of the South Saskatchewan river dam."
When the suggestion was made as to its being a vote of want of confidence in the government the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) rose in his place and said this should be a free vote. Now, possibly Liberal members from Saskatchewan could vote with the opposition in this matter, and it is possible that the amendment might not carry. But if the house had divided evenly and ten or twelve members had voted in that way, I can imagine the hon. member for Lake Centre and the Leader of the Opposition pointing the finger of scorn at the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), demanding his resignation and that we go to the country, because the house could not go into committee of supply.
The principle is the same. The house, composed as it is now, is probably different from what it would be if it were evenly divided. But I repeat that the principle is exactly the same; and I respectfully suggest that this would be a vote of want of confidence in the government.
There is only one other matter I should like to discuss. The report on the project was made and concurred in by P.F.R.A. authorities and by their consultants. In November of 1949, in a private conversation I had with the premier of Saskatchewan, he told me that the power possibilities of the South Saskatchewan were not nearly what had been anticipated when the previous estimates were made. At that time he was foreshadowing the appointment of Mr. Cass-Beggs so that he could bring in a report; and subsequently that report came in. The first doubt was then cast on the feasibility of the proposition as set out by P.F.R.A.
We now come to the next step. Since the federal government had a great deal of responsibility in the matter, and taking into

South Saskatchewan River Project consideration the doubts expressed by the premier of Saskatchewan, in view of the fact that there was some division of opinion it was considered necessary to arrive at a proper conclusion in the matter.
May I ask the hon. member a question? Does he know that the premier of Saskatchewan is prepared immediately to sign an agreement that the dam be proceeded with?

I am speaking of what happened in 1949, in private conversation with the premier of that province. As a result the Hogg commission was appointed and produced a report in which it did not negate the benefits of the project. Its main point was that the costs were so high as not to be economically sound.
A second point of confusion has been introduced into this matter. At the present time the people of Canada do not know whom to believe, and many members in the House of Commons are in the same position. During the debate many members from other parts of Canada have risen and said that while in principle they support the project, they do not know exactly what the present position is in respect of these varying and conflicting reports.
On top of this it is suggested that we should have a free vote. While I am not well versed in constitutional law, I do not see how the Prime Minister could have a free vote in the matter. The amendment is a vote of lack of confidence, and one either votes for or against the government. I feel this government is the only one that will ever build the project, if it is built; so I do not see why one should vote against it on this occasion.
I do not see what the advantage of a free vote would be, other than that a certain segment of members would vote to build the dam while another segment would vote against it. In my opinion the expression of opinion in the house this afternoon would indicate that such a motion could be lost, and if it were lost it would drive another spike into any possibility of success in the venture, so far as building the dam is concerned, and thus negate the whole proposal.
I do not see anything to be gained by the kind of vote suggested by the hon. member for Lake Centre. I think this afternoon we have done that which was absolutely necessary. As was pointed out by the Minister of Agriculture, the confusion that now exists has not had time to be cleared up. In my view this whole discussion is premature, and the investigation suggested this afternoon should have taken place before this debate.


The confusion that has developed in respect of figures, and other matters now beclouding the issue, should be resolved.
After the investigation has been made- and I hope it does not take too long-we will have arrived at the proper time to carry on our discussions and make decisions in the matter.

Mr. Speaker, I shall detain the house for only a moment or two, but I am bound to say a few words in view of the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing).
I have listened with interest throughout the debate, and feel it has been a most unusual one. We have heard lectures on Canadian unity; we have heard the suggestion by the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Studer) that thirteen members of the cabinet should be placed in limbo, and we have had other Liberal members from Saskatchewan stating that this subject is being treated as a political football. I have noticed, however, that they have been kicking the football around very gingerly.
I have risen particularly to refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart), I am sorry he is not now in his seat. I am always interested in listening to what he says because usually his observations are valuable. I believe he is a sincere member of the House of Commons. However, on occasions when he gets going under the full sail of his enthusiasm he goes a bit off course, especially when he deals with subjects such as smuggling and free votes in the House of Commons.
When the hon. member was speaking I asked him a question, when he had observed that so far as he was concerned he knew of nothing but free votes in the house. I drew his attention to the fact that in August of 1946 the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said, as reported at page 5431 of Hansard:
Nevertheless the government has no objection to an expression of opinion from the members of the house. I suggest that the vote should be a free expression regardless of party.
That statement was made in the debate on the milk subsidy. I questioned the hon. member because I thought the statement made at that time by the minister indicated clearly that there are votes which are not free expressions of opinions of members in the house.
The hon. member replied to my question with some ambiguity and, if I heard him correctly, stated, "I never heard of anything but a free vote. I voted"-and he was referring to this milk subsidy-"as I saw fit". Let

me draw the attention of the house to the fact that, according to Hansard of that date, August 27, 1946, the hon. member did not vote at all. I suppose he showed this usual independence and freedom of expression in not being present when the vote was called because even with a free vote there might have been some irritation on the government benches.
I am not personally acquainted with the area under discussion, with its physical features and the problems which must be solved. When it comes to a vote on this amendment I must base my decision upon what I have heard during this debate. I have heard all members from Saskatchewan in all parties suggest that this project should be proceeded with. I think if the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) really told the house what he thought he would say that the government should proceed with this project.
That does not necessarily mean the government is restricted to proceeding in this way or that way. I think the whole tenor of the debate has been that the people of Saskatchewan throughout the years have been led to believe that some action was going to be taken in this respect by the government. In speaking in favour of the amendment I am not going into details or suggesting that it should be done exactly in this way or in that way. We want to see the government satisfy the people of Saskatchewan by taking some action in this respect. Even though that action is limited action, it should be indicated by an item in the estimates.
This amendment simply states that there is no provision in the estimates for the building or the commencing of the South Saskatchewan river dam. Surely that is a most reasonable proposal. If all hon. members from Saskatchewan voted in favour of the amendment there would be no danger of the government being defeated. Therefore I shall support the amendment, because I believe the people of Saskatchewan have this action coming to them.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) said he was going to reply to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing).

Pardon me, on a point of order; as usual, the hon. member for Springfield has misunderstood what is being said in the house. I said that I was moved to speak by the hon. member for Vancouver South speaking previously.
South Saskatchewan River Project
I accept the humble apology of the hon. member. It' is quite evident that he has retracted what he indicated was his intention when he got up.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
How far off can a member
get?

You should know. I do not intend to take very long speaking on this matter as I know hon. members are anxious to have a vote on the main amendment moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). It comes to my mind that a serious attempt is being made by the Conservative and C.C.F. parties to force the government to say that they are going to go ahead with the building of this South Saskatchewan dam regardless of whether it is feasible. There are good reasons behind their attitude which I shall divulge in a minute or two.
We all know that only a few days ago a terrible disaster struck in Holland. Dikes which had been constructed for centuries were torn down by a terrific storm and people by the thousands were drowned. I believe the government of today is much concerned about a similar thing happening to the city of Saskatoon. I am not an engineer myself, but I think I can rely on the experience of the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson). If you are going to have a wall of water 190 feet high you must have a very good base to hold back that water. Every precaution must be taken before a project of this kind is taken on.
I imagine that in Holland they had the services of the best engineers in the country; nevertheless disaster overtook them. We must see that everything possible is done before this undertaking is started. I suggest that a committee of this house be set up with power to call engineers from different countries who have had experience in the building of similar dams. This afternoon the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Studer) told us of what had been accomplished in different countries by irrigation projects. It seems to me that before $100 million or $150 million, whatever the amount is, is spent, another few hundred dollars should be spent to bring engineers to this country who have had experience in this sort of thing.
There was a whisper on the wind some months ago that the Conservative party was looking for a new leader.
Why don't you apply?

I am more concerned that the rumour or the whisper on the wind that was going around seems to be true, because over the waves of the radio today we heard that

South Saskatchewan River Project this great member for Lake Centre is going to abandon Saskatchewan and seek a seat in Toronto. It is quite evident that his motive in moving the amendment in connection with the South Saskatchewan dam-

AFTER RECESS

Mr. Speaker, before the dinner adjournment I made the statement that the official opposition and the C.C.F. party were making a determined attempt to force the government to construct a dam on the South Saskatchewan river. I should like to read a short paragraph to be found at page 23 of the commission's report in the section dealing with recommendations and general considerations. It shows the magnitude of the construction that is required. Paragraph 52 reads as follows:
The four large earth structures-the main dam, the Coteau creek dam, the third meridian dam and the railway crossing-would require a total of
57.500.000	cubic yards of material, most of which can be obtained in the vicinity. The dam would be 205 feet high with a crest length of more than
8.000	feet from bank to bank. It would impound about 8 million acre-feet of water, of which
2.650.000	acre-feet would be live, or useful storage. The reservoir would extend 140 miles upstream on the South Saskatchewan river and thirty miles down the Qu'Appelle river valley to the third meridian. The reservoir would have a surface area of 116,000 acres and a shoreline of almost 500 miles. It would inundate about 70,000 acres of land of which 11 per cent is under cultivation.
To say the least, Mr. Speaker, that is a considerable undertaking. I hear the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) laughing. To him it is a laughing matter-
I was laughing at you.
To him it is a laughing matter if he can get the government of the country to spend $150 million which would not serve a useful purpose.
As long as it was on the dam it would be all right.

So far as I am able to gather, the dam would not be of very much value


to the hon. member for Assiniboia. The only value he is getting out of it is a little bit of political value. It would not make any difference whether the country spent three or four billion dollars as long as he was elected in his constituency. That is all he is worried about. I am going to ask him a sincere question. From his own standpoint as the operator of a farm, does he take the advice of men with practical experience or does he just throw their advice to the winds in the same way that he wanted to throw all copies of the report of the commission into the South Saskatchewan river? It does not make a particle of difference to him whether or not the project is economically sound.
I hope the government will consider seriously a suggestion I should like to put forward. I suggest that a committee of this house be set up to hear further recommendations and to call for persons who have had experience in building such dams in other countries. I am sure that the experience of men who have built such projects in other countries cannot help but be of value to us and at the same time, if it is at all possible to build the dam, it would pave the way toward doing that at an early date. We would also be sure of what we were doing.
As I said before dinner, not very long ago there was a terrific storm which smashed dikes in several places in the countries of Holland and England. I am told these dikes were not more than 40 feet high, but in the paragraph of the report which I quoted it is pointed out that in one place the dam will be 205 feet high. It will certainly require a solid structure and much engineering work to hold back that amount of water. I suggest to the hon. member for Assiniboia that if he has any respect for the dollars of the people of Canada, if he has any respect for the people who reside in Saskatoon, he will agree with me when I say that if the dam is built every possible step must be taken to make sure that the same conditions will not be created that were brought about in Europe a little while ago, which resulted in the drowning of several hundred people.
I am given to understand that the proposed dam will be about 60 miles almost directly south of Saskatoon. If that wall of water should be let loose we all know what would happen to the people of that city. Therefore the government or whoever builds the dam will have to be very careful that the dam is sound in structure, and make sure before starting that it is economically possible.

What did the P.F.R.A. engineers
say?

Mr. Speaker, before the dinner recess I listened with interest to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing) discussing this project. He mentioned that as the member for Yale I could tell the house something about irrigation. However, I am afraid from the statements he made that he arrived at the wrong conclusion. As the member for Yale, which is an area possibly more advanced in irrigation than any other part of North America, I can say from my own experience that I think the South Saskatchewan river project should be proceeded with regardless of the cost. I say that because my memory goes back 30 years to the time we faced a similar problem of whether or not to go ahead with an irrigation scheme. I remember well that some papers opposed the scheme. They said it was impractical and that the cost would be too great. They said that a cost of up to $30 an acre for irrigation would break the farmers.
Looking back over those 30 years I well remember the type of land that was involved, covered with sagebrush and in some cases not even capable of sustaining that sagebrush. It was being sold or offered for sale for $5 an acre. A lot of it was bought at that price and some at $10 or $15 an acre. Last summer I was in that same district. It has been irrigated now for about 20 or 25 years. Orchards with young trees on land that was formerly worth only $5 or $10 an acre are selling at $2,000 an acre. That has all been brought about by the application of natural water to good land.
The same condition prevails in the area of the Palliser triangle. I believe that if good water can be applied to that land at a reasonable figure the same success can be achieved. I know that in some cases our irrigation cost ran from $15 to $25 an acre, which may be considered high. But as the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing) pointed out, the average income per acre on our land is $1,000, so we could well pay that cost. However, if the crops on the prairie are not so lucrative or do not return such a high figure, I claim that alfalfa, beets and crops of that type could very well bear the cost of the figures stated here today, $6 or $7 an acre.
I am satisfied that this scheme would well repay the government in five, ten or twenty years. As it is that life-giving water, that wonderful stream is emptying itself into the ocean and is of no value. You cannot recover next year or in twenty years what you miss this year. It is a matter of taking steps immediately to apply that water to the land to make the central part of Saskatchewan a prosperous area, giving those farmers who 68108-116
South Saskatchewan River Project are now applying to leave the district an opportunity to make a livelihood.
I am speaking now from real experience because I have seen worse land, covered with sagebrush, brought into production and bearing crops second to none on the North American continent. I heartily approve of the scheme, and 1 would like to point out that practically every member from British Columbia, knowing the experience we have had, would give full support to any steps the government care to take to implement this scheme.
I realize that the cost is great and that the government hesitates on that account, possibly because of the fear of repercussions from the rest of Canada; but I can assure them that as far as British Columbia is concerned we will give full support to any scheme the government may deem fit and proper, and that it would be prepared to undertake.

My hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. George) wants to know what a free vote is. I ask him to consult the Minister

South Saskatchewan River Project of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) who, on that occasion, announced to the house that it was the wish of the government that the vote on that occasion be a free vote. I may tell him, since he was not here on that occasion, that the result of that announcement that it was a free vote was that some Liberals voted one way and some voted the other, and the final result was that the amendment carried. Nevertheless the government was not defeated. It was not a vote of confidence or of non-confidence because the minister, speaking on behalf of the government, had stated that it would not be so treated.
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to review again the circumstances surrounding what happened in 1946 but for the interjection that came a moment ago. Rather I rose to remind the house of what happened more recently, namely on June 12, 1951. On that occasion when the motion that the house go into committee of supply was made, as is so often the case, by our genial friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) moved an amendment. It was an amendment which had to do with a proposal that a select committee be set up to consider the rules of this house. It was an amendment preceded by the usual preamble:
That all the words alter the word "that" to the end ol the question be struck out and that the following be substituted therefor:
Immediately after the Leader of the Opposition spoke to that amendment, a speech that occupied about four pages of Hansard, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) rose and said, as reported at page 3966 of Hansard of June 12, 1951:
Mr. Speaker, the government, and I am sure most members, if not all members of the house, welcome at least the substance of the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew).
The Prime Minister went on to say:
Before declaring expressly that we should be glad to accept it, I should like to see the exact language that is used.
Then about a page further on the Prime Minister said:
I have now had an opportunity of reading the language of the motion submitted by the Leader of the Opposition. I take it that the Leader of the Opposition does not intend this motion as one of no confidence in the government.
Then Hansard records this line:

Oh, no.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, it having been made clear on that occasion that it was not intended by the Leader of the Opposition that that motion was to be regarded as one of nonconfidence in the government, the Prime Minister in the name of the government accepted


the motion. So, after a few more members had spoken, we find on page 3971 of Hansard of that same date this notation:
Amendment (Mr. Drew) agreed to.
Mr. Speaker, the government did not fall. It had already been made clear on both sides that this was not a motion of non-confidence, that this was something concerning which there was general agreement throughout the house. Instead of the government falling, Hansard goes on to say:

speechtext:
I move that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself again into committee of supply.
After a bit of debate that motion was carried. We went into supply and went on with the business of the house.
Now, I submit, Mr. Speaker, that although there is one difference between that situation and this, there is also an element of great similarity. The difference is that on that occasion the debate was quite harmonious and on this occasion there has been a fair amount of acrimony. But the similarity is also there, namely on that occasion it was pointed out from both sides that there was general agreement on what was asked for in the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition.
The same thing holds true now. There is agreement in all parts of the house. There is agreement on the part of members representing all parts of Canada that we want this project gone ahead with, that we want the dam on the South Saskatchewan river to be built. It has also been made clear by the hon. member for Lake Centre, who moved the amendment, that he does not desire it to be regarded as a motion of non-confidence in the government. He desires rather that it should be treated as an amendment dealing with the subject matter of that amendment itself, and that the question of confidence in the government and the right of the government to go into supply be dealt with immediately thereafter.
So, Mr. Speaker, my purpose in rising is to express the hope that the Prime Minister will at this stage catch the mood of the house, as it were, and realize that there is support in all parts of the house for-and I quote his words of June 12, 1951-
-at least the substance of the amendment moved by-
-the opposition. If he would be prepared to do that, obviously the house need not be divided. The amendment can be accepted and it can be, thereby, an expression of

South Saskatchewan River Project
opinion by the house in favour of the substance of the amendment, in favour of going ahead with the South Saskatchewan project. Immediately after that has been dealt with in that way the Minister of Public Works can get up again, as he did on June 12, 1951, and move that we then go into committee of supply.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that members and supporters of the government cannot have it both ways. On June 12, 1951, they claimed that if there was something upon which they were all agreed, it could be treated as a motion that was not a want of confidence motion. But today, in February, 1953, they try to claim that a similar motion must be regarded as a want of confidence motion. If the government insists, Mr. Speaker, in regarding this as a motion of non-confidence, in the light of that precedent of June 12, 1951, it simply means the government is really against the immediate construction of the dam as requested in the amendment that is now before the house.
I submit that any attempt on the part of Liberals, such as we have had during the course of this debate, to find an excuse for voting against this amendment on the ground it has something to do with confidence, is put out of court by the precedent to which I have referred on June 12, 1951. I made an appeal yesterday to the backbenchers on the Liberal side to ask for a free vote such as we had in August, 1946. They have not seen fit to do that, so the possibility of such a free vote being announced is, I take it, rather slim.
Therefore, since that course has not been followed, I now make this appeal to the government, that they treat this subject in the same way as they treated the question of a committee on the rules in 1951. It is a different matter, I know. The scope of this motion may be much greater; but there is this similarity, that on that occasion we were all agreed and so the motion was allowed to pass. On this occasion we are all agreed, so the amendment should be allowed to pass so the house can express its general support of this proposition and get on with the business of going into supply.

Mr. Speaker, I was paired with the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). Had I voted, I would have voted for the amendment.

I rise because of the emergency now facing the sugar beet growers not only in Ontario but in the three provinces of Alberta, Manitoba and Quebec. Another reason for my rising tonight is the recent announcement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) at Havana, Cuba, within the last few days, as reported in the press. I shall quote briefly from the press report, as follows:
Right Hon. C. D. Howe, Canada's trade minister, said yesterday that Canada and Cuba may be able to work out a new sugar agreement when the current one expires soon, but it would have to be one based on an understanding of "our respective problems and difficulties."
The main point there is the fact that this sugar agreement between Canada and Cuba does not expire until the end of this year, and unless an agreement is arranged between these two countries on a satisfactory basis r.ow there will be no sugar beets grown in any province of Canada, nor will there be any refinery operating in Canada this year.
That is the reason for the urgent endeavour to again present this matter which concerns so many people in Canada, not only the sugar beet growers but also the people in the cities, towns and villages, as well as new immigrants who have come to this country and got their start in the sugar beet fields with a hope of continuing in that line of work in the future.
In order that we might bring this matter up to date, without going into too long a review I would say that in May of 1951 Canada and Cuba entered into an agreement whereby Canada was to take 75,000 tons of raw sugar a year for the years 1951, 1952 and 1953, and in return Cuba was to take more seed potatoes, wheat flour and codfish. I think it is fair to say that every member in the House of Commons desires to promote


trade with other countries; but I do not think it would be the wish of anyone in the house that we should enter into an arrangement of this nature which would prejudice people in our country, or in the country with whom we are dealing.
The month of February is now one-third over, and we know that farmers across Canada who plan producing sugar beets in the coming season are wondering whether they should buy fertilizer and sugar beet seed, and whether they should sign contracts with the processors for the production of sugar beets. I have been in several sugar beet producing areas and they are very much upset, particularly in the last few days, as a result of this announcement; because since the agreement was entered into between this country and Cuba we find that, for the first time since 1931 or 1932, Cuba delivered to the Canadian market in the first eleven months of last year slightly more than 31 million pounds of refined sugar.
I wish to be fair by stating that I do not think it was the intention of this government or of officials in the Department of Trade and Commerce, when they entered into an agreement with Cuba to take 75,000 tons of raw sugar, that we would be subjected to importations of such enormous amounts of refined sugar. True enough, as I pointed out when I spoke a few days after the opening of the session in November, the department had been warned by the growers' association in 1948 and 1949 that as soon as the sugar control was over the growers might be subjected to pressure from Cuba, especially if, by chance, there was overproduction in that country.
It is a matter of record that in 1952 Cuba had a record crop of about 8 million tons of sugar. As we know, she is the greatest sugar-producing country in the world, and her record crop in that year placed her in a position where she wanted to get rid of her surplus. While for the current year her quota has been set back to some 5,500,000 tons, nevertheless there is enough held over from 1952 to stand as a threat to this country by reason of the fact that at the moment there is nothing to prevent her shipping refined sugar into Canada.
I think we must regard the agreement as one that was entered into in good faith. True enough there have been people throughout Canada who have said that our government blundered and that the sugar beet growers were sold down the river. Let me say here that the sugar beet growers of this country, in an industry now 52 or 53 years old, have not had the tariff changed on sugar since about 1922 or 1923. Since that time the two old parties have been in power, and seven

parliaments have come and gone without any change in that tariff. So there may be some reasonable excuse in the minds of those who negotiated the agreement with Cuba for overlooking the possibility that Cuba, facing a crisis in her country because of that overproduction, would endeavour to find an outlet for that production in Canada.
The situation we find today is that Cuba finds in Canada a potential market for refined sugar. Let there be no mistake about that. I still say that when the agreement was entered into I think it was done in good faith. It was a contract between two countries. In order to stimulate trade we agreed to take 75,000 tons of raw sugar, and that was a new market for Cuba. She was very anxious indeed to obtain an outlet in Canada for her crop, and we were in the position that we wanted to expand our trade not only with Cuba but with other countries.
We must look at the problem in true perspective. I am not one who advocates tariffs, or high trade walls. I think hon. members will agree with me that in these days it is necessary for governments in different countries to negotiate trade agreements around the conference table. We have seen the United States avail herself of provisions which to our minds are not fair and which, as a matter of fact, have been unfair to Canada. I say one way to come to a satisfactory agreement with Cuba or with any other country is by the officials of Canada and that country sitting around a conference table and entering into a contract that will not prejudice the farmers and producers of either country.
Here we find an industry that has stood on its feet for 52 years. It has faced two crises and is now facing a third. The first was in the thirties when Cuba was shipping into Canada about 40 million pounds of sugar a year. The next crisis was when we were at war. Because of the small production of sugar beets in Ontario at that time the leader of this party, who was then premier of Ontario, gave the sugar beet growers in that province three-quarters of a million dollars in order that Canadians might have a little larger sugar ration. During that time boats loaded with sugar were sunk off our shores, but the sugar beet industry overcame that particular crisis and made a terrific contribution during that war.
I contend that we should never put ourselves in the position, whether we are in a cold or hot war, where we must depend upon any foreign country for our supplies of a necessity such as sugar. It should never be the policy of any government to crucify or sell any industry down the river. I said
Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement in November, and I say it again, that when you crucify any segment of our primary producers it affects the economy of the whole country.
This industry has meant a great deal to this country in many ways. It has established many new Canadians and has room for more. I do not want any member in this house to say that we are at the limit of our production. Our refineries are efficient and are capable of refining more sugar than is grown in Canada today. Just offhand I would say that the modern refineries in this country-one of the most modern in the world is in Alberta; the ones in Chatham are older but are quite efficient-have a capacity of about one-third more than is now being produced.
This is the crucial time for sugar beet growers in every province throughout Canada because they must plan ahead. They cannot wait until the end of this agreement, until the end of 1953; they cannot wait until March. If they are going to put in sugar beets this year in any province they must make their contracts now. They have not made those contracts with the processors. I say tonight that because of the agreement with Cuba, as far as these contracts are concerned there will not be any sugar beets grown in Canada nor will there be a refinery operating in this country.
Last fall just before navigation closed some 30 million pounds of refined sugar came into Canada. Between January 19 and January 26 some million and a quarter pounds entered London and Toronto, the markets usually supplied by the processors in Chatham and Wallaceburg.
I do not want to be provincial in this matter, but I am concerned about the people in Ontario. There are nine counties representing some 12 or 14 ridings in Ontario where sugar beets are produced. The farmers have a huge investment. They have equipment and machinery which is good for nothing else but sugar beet growing. If they cannot be assured of some reasonable market for their product they will not grow sugar beets and then we might well be dependent upon some foreign country for our requirements.
I want to make it plain that we in this country over the years have taken raw sugar from empire countries, and a certain amount from other countries as well. We entered into a contract with Cuba in good faith and then we find Cuba selling not only the quota provided for, but unloading on the Ontario market some 30 million pounds. Just as soon as navigation opens Cuba will make

Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement more sugar available and ships will be going to the head of the lakes and the western market will be flooded.
We know that today enough sugar beets are produced in Manitoba and Alberta to nearly take care of the requirements of Canada west of the great lakes. There will not be a sugar beet grown west of the great lakes unless we come to an agreement now. We cannot wait until March or April, much less until next year, as that disturbing article seems to indicate to the people of this country.
Cuba was quite aware of what she was doing. She is not averse to protecting her own economy. I saw an article which appeared in a Cuban newspaper commenting upon the speech I made in November. The important part of the whole speech as far as I was concerned was the determination by that country to consolidate her gain. I said in November that Cuba's refining capacity was sufficient to supply Canada's needs twice over.
We want to be fair with Cuba. We are ready to tell Cuba tomorrow that we will take her raw sugar in any quantity that is fair and reasonable, but if her refined sugar is sent in our primary producers will be crucified and sold down the river. I think Cuba entered into the agreement in good faith, but found a way out. She found a vulnerable market in Canada. Most of her production goes to the United States.
Let me say here that we have increased our exports to Cuba of some articles in short supply, including copper. We must remember that today the United States has a huge rearmament program. She has an entree into Cuba that no other country in the world has because of her preference duty. Cuba supplies the United States with about half of her production of sugar. She also supplies some refined sugar, but both the refined and the raw are on a quota basis. There is no misunderstanding about the arrangement between the United States and Cuba. She ships in her refined and she ships in her raw sugar, but the growers and processors in the United States know how much is going to come in from Cuba each year.
Let us emphasize the fact that last year Cuba had a record crop. We must recognize also that she wanted to get rid of that crop. She wanted to sell it for dollars; she did not want to sell it for sterling. Canada was the vulnerable market, and she got in here. I do not for one minute suggest that we should avail ourselves of tariff protection. I want to emphasize and I want hon. members to understand that I think the way to increase

trade between nations today is for the responsible people in various governments to sit around the conference table and negotiate trade agreements. Let it be done in no other way.
We want to expand our trade. I am happy the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is making a trip to South America. We want to expand our trade with those countries. They have many products that we need. In our great industrial development we can use many tropical and semi-tropical products. It is quite apparent that our trade with many of these countries has increased a great deal. We are on the eve of a great industrial development in this country, greater perhaps than we have ever dreamed of. We will require many of the products of these tropical and semi-tropical countries.
There is no reason in the world why Cuba should not sit down at the conference table, because she did turn over 75,000 tons of sugar a year for three years. We did not take it all in 1951, but what we did not take in that year we took in 1952. In addition we took in refined sugar in 1952. As I see it, the picture that is developing is most dangerous. The minute navigation opens there will be boatloads of Cuban sugar coming into Montreal and great lakes ports, and the refineries in the maritimes, Montreal, Ontario, Manitoba and Alberta, will not open their doors this fall.
I think it is time there should be some understanding and some assurance given by the government rather than Liberal members going around the country and saying "What is 2 per cent? The amount we get from Cuba is only 2 per cent of our requirements." It is true enough that the amount of refined sugar that came into Canada from Cuba is 2 per cent of our requirements. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. MacKenzie), the hon. member for Kent, Ont. (Mr. Huffman) and the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. McCubbin) have all said in speaking to various growers in the different areas that it is only a small detail, that it is only 2 per cent of our requirements.
It is only 2 per cent per capita, but that 2 per cent comes into the Ontario market where we have been shipping our own product from the refineries in Wallaceburg and Chatham. We know today for a fact that the big buyers of these products from these two refineries have told the processors that they will not want their product again unless there is a strike or a war. That is the situation in which we find ourselves, and that is the situation that is going to be found all across Canada. It is not enough for private

members to go around making statements. This is a matter for government deliberation, and now.
By the end of this month these farmers will want to know whether or not they should prepare their soil and make contracts for sugar beets. The people with whom I have come in contact are determined that they are not going to grow sugar beets until there is some assurance that there will be a reasonable market. They have competed over all these years. They have competed with sugar at $3 and some odd cents a hundred f.o.b. Montreal. They have competed when it was $10.50 f.o.b. Montreal. They have competed against raw sugar from any country in the world, but they are not in a position to compete with refined sugar. When it means crucifying that industry why should that be expected?
We can make a fair contract with Cuba by taking raw sugar. Cuba says it does not want our flour, that it will take our wheat and refine it. We say to Cuba: All right, we too have the capacity to refine sugar. You keep your refined sugar and send us the raw. It has been suggested that if necessary we should take an extra 15,000 or 20,000 tons of raw sugar. All well and good. Let the agreement be signed, but signed now. We cannot afford to wait. What is disturbing to some of the growers are the statements that have been made by some members who have been belittling their efforts and who probably do not realize the situation in which the growers find themselves. Some have said that all this protest is promoted by someone else.
After I spoke the last time I think it was the hon. member for Lambton-Kent who was kind enough to say that Cuba surely had lots of sugar and had such a tremendous crop that it tried to unload a few boatloads in Canada. The few boatloads that were unloaded in Canada disturbed the sugar beet growers in these areas in western Ontario.
A great deal can be said on this subject. In the main I do not intend to repeat what I said last November because that speech was followed by several others that dealt quite effectively with the serious situation facing the primary producers of sugar. What disturbs the growers today is the uncertainty. They are more or less disappointed, and are on the brink of bankruptcy because they do not know what the policy of the government is. We have government spokesmen going around saying that the government is going to take care of them. That statement applies to the members to whom I referred a few moments ago. I should like to refer to an article that appeared in the Windsor Daily Star of February 6 dealing with certain
Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement remarks made by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent when speaking in the city of Sarnia. The hon. member is reported as saying:
I know the present situation is unfortunate for the growers, but I don't know what the future holds.
The article continues as follows:
If nothing can be accomplished, Mr. MacKenzie said, "I think we should try to tide the industry over, for we want to save the beet industry and we won't let it be thrown to the wolves."
The hon. member objected to my statement in November when I said that the industry was being sold down the river, but he does not mind saying that the industry is being thrown to the wolves. The article continues as follows:
He pointed out that duty charged on the importation of refined sugar is $1.89 a hundredweight, plus, if such is the case, a dumping duty of 75 cents a hundredweight.
There is no dumping of Cuban sugar into Canada; let that be understood. I hope the press of this country will not again say that when the representatives of the industry were here in October to see government officials, they suggested there was dumping by Cuba. When the hon. member for Kent, Ont., spoke last fall he was dismayed at my reference to this statement, but I should like to refer him now to the Montreal Gazette of October 24. As a matter of fact, I think the report was in practically all papers in Canada as well as in the New York Times of that date and the day after. In fact it was in the New York paper before the deputation even arrived home. I want it understood without any doubt now that when the delegation came to Ottawa not one delegate referred to the dumping of Cuban sugar into Canada.
As we know, dumping means that Cuba would sell to Canada at a lesser price than she was selling for home consumption. Cuba today sells all her refined sugar through one single administrator, a quasi-government official, and there are three prices. Cuba sells in New York at 2 cents a pound or $2 a hundred more than the price at which they sell to Canada, and they have a lower price for their domestic consumption, which only amounts to about 2 or 3 per cent of their total production. Therefore we would never be in a position to impose any dumping duty.
But I say that is not the solution to the problem in any case. Many responsible people * of the area of western Ontario about which I have been speaking have been members of the association for years. I can refer, for instance, to Eugene King of Kent county. I think he was president of the sugar beet growers' association. I can refer to Cameron

Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement McTaggart, who is a director of the association. They say that the situation is alarming. These are responsible men. One is in the county of Kent and the other is in the county of Middlesex. Some of these people have grown sugar beets for 35 or 40 years. They say they have never faced such a crisis before.
They are hoping they will not lose their huge investments, and that their routine of producing sugar will be carried on without any interruption through government action or inaction. I have great respect for men like King, McTaggart and others who have followed the progress of this industry for the past 35 or 40 years. They are greatly disturbed.
I should like to refer now to an editorial in the Detroit Free Press of Monday, February 2. I think I expressed this idea in a different form a few months ago, but it sums it up. The editorial is on page 8 and carries the heading "National interest should determine tariff action". It reads in part as follows:
At the same time this country-
The reference is to the United States.
*-would not be the gainer if industries vital to its security were sacrificed and we again became wholly dependent on foreign sources for critical goods.
Mr. Speaker, if I did not say anything else tonight and quoted only that paragraph it would be, after all is said and done, the gist of my argument here. Let us not sacrifice an industry that is so important to our economy, that may mean so much to us in the future as it does today. It may mean more in the event of a shooting war. We are in a position today where we can supply at least part of our requirements.
That being the case, Mr. Speaker, with the gradual development of our country, with the hope these people have for making a livelihood and making their contribution to Canada, let us not at this time through action or inaction, intentionally or otherwise, sacrifice an industry which has meant so much to the economy of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I very much regret the fact that this discussion has been brought on by my hon. friend from Lambton West (Mr. Murphy). The agreement to which he has made reference is the only agreement I know of that has been made in the last few years under which we in the maritime provinces could look forward to any beneficial results. I believe that the New Brunswick members will agree with that statement, as will other maritime members.
This agreement was made by the minister and the government in the belief that it


would provide some markets for salt fish. The hon. member for Lambton West mentioned that. It was to cover not only salt fish but included canned fish, potatoes, smoked fish and many other products of the maritimes. At that time we found it very difficult to obtain markets in other parts of the world. This scheme was arranged, and it has been of great benefit to our fishermen. In the northern part of the province, in that part which my hon. friend for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) comes from, there are a great many producers of salt cod. The same applies to Newfoundland, the same applies to Nova Scotia, and the same applies to Prince Edward Island. This scheme has been a great help.
Only a few months ago the hon. member who has spoken, and many of his colleagues who sit with him, were condemning this government for its lack of interest in so far as the cost of living was concerned. They said the government was not doing anything at all to try to stop the rise in the cost of living. I believe these same members must agree that the price of sugar today has dropped. Surely they are not advocating at this time that the consumers should pay $1.50 or $2 a hundred more in order to protect these few sugar beet growers. In other words, the hon. member for Lambton West has suggested that 2 per cent of the sugar consumed in Canada is all that is involved in this agreement.
No, no, not in the agreement.
The consumption.

That is what I said, 2 per cent of the consumption of sugar in Canada. If 2 per cent of the sugar consumption in Canada is responsible for prosperity or otherwise in the maritime provinces, surely we should expect to receive some consideration. This agreement has been helpful to each and every maritime province. It has been an encouragement to the producers down there.

On a point of order, I know the hon. member would not want the record to be left as he is giving it. I want to make it clear that we have never complained about the agreement for the 75,000 tons of raw sugar. What is disturbing the market today is refined sugar coming on it, and the likelihood of that sugar taking care of all of our requirements, which would thereby sacrifice and crucify our industry. The price of sugar is determined by the world sugar price in New York.

I might add to that a suggestion of my own. If they can send refined sugar in here at prices lower than

we can refine it in Canada, then there is something wrong with our refineries at home.
Hear, hear.

I believe, if you look into the situation, that a great deal of the difficulty lies with the refineries we have in the Dominion of Canada. They could sell a lot cheaper, and they will get the price down when they are forced to it; but so long as they get the protection which the hon. member for Lambton West would like to see they will take advantage of that protection and the consumers of this country will pay the bill.
Hear, hear.

I am one who takes a pretty strong stand on this particular question, as members of the house know. I will make one other statement. During the last ten years this continent has pumped billions and billions of dollars into other countries to try to rehabilitate them, to put them into a position where they can stand on their own feet and live the way we believe people should live. Already there is the idea in this country of sticking up tariff walls. In other words, you give with one hand and take away with the other.
Well, I cannot subscribe to that kind of doctrine and I hope members of this government cannot be convinced that it is a proper course to follow. What we need in this country and in every democratic country in the world is a freer movement of goods back and forth between those countries. I want to suggest that if we ever hope or expect to have world peace in this world it will never be brought about by tariff walls. When you set one part of the world against another, and when one country says that its country must have protection, then it will hang itself.
I think we have to make it clear that if a business cannot stand on its own feet it should not exist. That might be a pretty broad statement, but if an industry cannot survive without subsidies, then there is something wrong. I realize that people in this sugar industry are very much concerned, and that they are very much interested in their own livelihood; but I wonder whether, if it were gone into carefully, we might not find that the answer to this problem does not lie with the sugar beet producers but rather with the manufacturers in our factories. I believe we are in a position in this country to refine sugar as cheaply as they can do it in Cuba. If that is not so, I would like to have some explanation why it costs more to refine sugar in this country than it does down there.
Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement
Again, I want to say that all the maritime provinces-and I will include Newfoundland because now we have four maritime provinces-as I have said on many occasions in this chamber, are most dependent on these American markets. Take them away from us and our economy is completely wrecked. The hon. member who just spoke used these words, and I jotted them down: "sold down the river"; "thrown to the wolves" and "crucified". We would be all three if these markets were taken from us.

Your own member said
"thrown to the wolves".
On a question of privilege, I said this government did not want to see the beet industry thrown to the wolves.
That is what I said.
No, the hon. member for Lambton West said the sugar beet growers had been sold down the river, quite a different thing.

I do not know just what description would fit but, as I said before, if this agreement were interfered with in any way it would certainly mean selling those in the maritime provinces down the river. We do not get very many subsidies down there, and we do not get very much financial assistance. We are quite an understanding people, and we try to stand on our own feet. We are willing to produce what we have to produce in competition with any part of the world. If we cannot produce fish as cheaply as someone else, then let us eat someone else's fish. If we cannot produce sugar as cheaply as we can buy it somewhere else, then let us give the consumer the advantage of cheaper living.
We have heard right in this chamber, and I have sat and listened to it day after day, that the government was inactive as far as the cost of living was concerned; but the very first time the consumer is able to buy a little cheaper there are hon. members on their feet wanting protection.
I had not intended saying very much when I got up tonight, but I could not refrain from saying what I have said and I hope that my friends from New Brunswick will do likewise. I see the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery) and the hon. member for Gloucester are both in their seats. Those counties are producers of potatoes which are sold to Cuba and other countries to the south of us. I do not believe those hon. members will get on their feet and support the suggestion made tonight by the hon. member for Lambton West. They talk about putting government members on the spot, and we

Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement were supposed to have been put on the spot this afternoon; but I should like to see some of the New Brunswick members, who are in the same situation I am, get up and honestly express their feelings with regard to the agreement we have with Cuba.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.
Are you aware that two of your own members, the hon. member for Kent, Ont. (Mr. Huffman) and the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. MacKenzie) asked for quotas when they spoke?
That is not a question, that is a statement, Mr. Speaker. So far as quotas are concerned-
We would like to know what government policy is.

-if we can buy
sugar cheaper in Cuba than we can buy it somewhere else, why not give the Canadian consumer the advantage?

I rise tonight, Mr. Speaker, because I am a producer and always have been. I am getting rather fed up with members getting up in this house and requesting that the primary producer bear the brunt of the burden in reducing the cost of living.
Can it be done any other way?

That is all very well, but if you take profitable production away from the primary producer what are you going to have left? As soon as the primary producer cannot produce at a profit, then of course the manufacturer gets tied up. He cannot sell his goods and his labouring staff is cut. These employees are then sent back to the country, where a lot of them should have remained in the first place.
Let us hear you bring it down.

The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing), following a speech by the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) last fall, got up in this house and said that the cost of living was coming down. At whose expense did it come down?
He did a good job.

Who bore the brunt of that reduction in the cost of living? It was the primary producer who bore every cent of it. You believe that the burden of reducing the cost of living should be borne by the primary producer in this country.
[Mr. Stuart (Charlotte) .1
Lumber and fish are cheap.

I got my first training in a county council, and I am going to read you a resolution passed by the council of the county of Huron, of which I was a member. The resolution reads:
Resolution passed by the Huron county council in January session, January 23, 1953
The council of Huron county wishes to point out to the Canadian government that growers' returns for sugar beets and other payments made by the processors to factory and weigh station workmen, railways, truckers, etc., are a valuable source of revenue in the integrated economy of our community. In the last three years this industry has contributed, on the average, $11 million per year in southwestern Ontario.
Our urban and farmer citizens understand that the Ontario beet sugar industry which has thrived for half a century, will probably not operate next year unless some measures are adopted to stop the flood of foreign refined sugar which has deprived the Ontario made product of its traditional home markets of Toronto, Hamilton, Windsor.
Without the menace of foreign refined sugar, the domestic beet sugar industry heretofore has had a surge market within its own country. In these days of international instability this is the only market we can control. There has never been a surplus of beet sugar, and until now growers have been assured of a cash return for every ton of their crop harvested.
Besides the stability of this domestic industry, the part it played during food-short war years will never be forgotten. Ontario grown beet sugar was badly needed by Canadian consumers when submarines effectively stopped inbound boats carrying cane sugar from the tropics. The war emergency need for this domestic source of supply may occur again.
For these reasons, which are a few of many, we the council of Huron county unanimously beseech the government to take whatever steps are necessary in stopping foreign refined sugar produced by cheap native labour from ruining Ontario's beet sugar industry.
There is a resolution which comes from the county of Huron, one of the best counties in Ontario or the Dominion of Canada. I have another resolution which comes from the town of Exeter, so you can see that all the representations are not from the primary producers. These people realize that if the flow of money to the primary producer is cut off, then of course they suffer. There is no man, woman or child, I do not care where they live, who is not dependent entirely on the primary producer. Anyone who gets up in this house and says that the primary producer should bear the brunt of the reduction in the cost of living is just crazy.
You want 2 cents protection on sugar?
No, I just want a fair deal on sugar.

Tell us what it is; how much
protection?

I shall tell you in a minute if you will keep quiet long enough. If the importation of Cuban refined sugar were stopped, Canada still would have excellent trade relations with Cuba on the basis of her raw sugar imports of 75,000 tons a year, without buying a single pound of refined sugar from Cuba. The current raw sugar concession to Cuba is a valuable one, as Cuba could not have sold one pound of raw sugar to Canadian refiners if the government, this government you are talking about, had not arranged to rebate to the refiners, at a cost to the public, a sufficient amount to equalize the laid-down cost of Cuban raw sugar with that of empire raw sugar which comes into Canada under preferential tariff rates. So it follows that our trade relations with Cuba could have been maintained on the basis of the 75,000 tons of raw sugar annually. Not one single pound of refined sugar from Cuba need enter Canada.
I have only about 300 growers in my section of the country, but I am sure the rest of the population in that section would not want those 300 growers to absorb the shock of the difference in the price the consumer would have to pay for sugar. There is no other industry that is in competition with the sugar beet industry. It does not interfere with anybody else. We only produce about 20 per cent or less than 25 per cent of the country's requirements. Sugar beets do not interfere with any other crop. Why penalize an industry that has flourished for the last 50 years for the sake of allowing Cuban refined sugar to enter this market? It will put these fellows out of business. I think it is ridiculous. I do not know whether anything can be done about it.
I introduce this subject now, but I hope it will not get into the same position as the Saskatchewan dam did during the last few days. The only reason I have spoken tonight was to help our friends on the government side of the house. I am trying to present a case in their favour.
Will the hon. member permit a question? Is he aware that Lethbridge, Alberta, which is the sugar centre of the west, pays the highest per capita income tax in the Dominion of Canada?
Why?
If I may be permitted to answer, Mr. Speaker, I think it may be because sugar is a very productive crop and a very profitable crop.
Did you ever grow sugar beets?

No; they do not grow in my area.
Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement

If you had to grow and take care of one-half acre of them, there would not be very many sugar beets grown. I have grown sugar beets. I know how much work is involved. It is for that reason I want to read you part of another resolution, a copy of which I received from some of our new Canadians. It reads as follows:
We, the new Dutch and Belgian immigrant farmers who soon will become Canadian citizens of the parish of Parkhill, wish to tender our support to your government and particularly to the Hon. C. D. Howe, whom we hope and pray will intercede on our behalf when on his mission to the Cuban government, in order to give us some protection from the influx of Cuban refined white sugar which has been so detrimental to the beet sugar industry of Ontario, with a resultant drop in the price of beets to the producer.
These fellows came from Europe. They are hard workers. They are about the only labourers you can get to go into the sugar beet fields. Those of you who know anything about growing sugar beets know what a strenuous job it is. The job does not last for only a week or two. It starts as soon as the beets are ready to be thinned out. You have to get down almost on your hands and knees to thin them out, because they will not thrive if there are two in the one place. They have to be thinned out so that there is only one in the one spot. Then you have to keep the weeds out. It is a strenuous job all summer. Then you come to the fall, and if you happen to get a dry fall and good weather you do not have too much difficulty, but very often they have to take the sugar beets right out of the mud; they have to take them out of the snow, and under adverse conditions.
The growers of sugar beets are not interfering with anybody else, and the beets do not interfere with any other crop. Why the government would not protect the primary producer in this regard is something I cannot understand. It is typical of this government, of course. Perhaps I should not condemn them yet because the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has not returned. He may come back with a very favourable solution to the whole problem. I should not say that the Cubans have been sending in this sugar thoughtlessly. It has been coming in legitimately. They have paid the tariff on it, and we cannot very well stop it coming in. But surely there is some way of stopping it. I know that not so very long ago when shirts were dumped- in this country by Japan that was quickly stopped. If the primary producers wanted a few of those shirts they could not buy them. It is terrible when the sugar producers want some protection for their commodity.
