I do not intend to go over the ground that was covered by my good friend the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy). Perhaps I have said enough about sugar. The fact remains that the sugar beet growers are not the only primary producers of this country who are being affected at the present time. There are the dairymen; they are primary producers, too. They have been having a tough time, due in part at least to the fact that cheap oils were allowed to come into Canada. Something should have been done about that before we lost all our markets. Last year our cheese men were almost put out of business because they could not sell any cheese, and we imported more cheese than we exported. We had tons of it here that we could not sell. I do not know what kind of policy that is.
I turn from there to the hog policy that we have had to work under for the last four or five years. We have not had a hog policy at all. If it was the policy of the government to put the hog producers out of business, they certainly made a good job of it.
Don't get too far afield from what you are talking about.
I should like to tell the minister a few of the things that are happening.
You are wrong in all of them.

I am not wrong in all of them.
I am going to quote a few.
Pigs are 25 cents higher now than they were before Christmas.
Keep quiet and you might learn something. A year ago a primary producer of hogs in Ontario had 34 brood sows; today he has 12.
The way the price is going now he will wish he had them all back againi
If the price had gone the way you wanted it to go it would have been down to 23 cents.
No; I kept faith.

Then we have another hog grower out in Alberta who a year ago had 67 hogs. Today he has none. That is typical of what is happening all over the country. Let me take an example a little nearer home. Down in Quebec there are three parishes that took a survey a year ago, and I can name them.
I thought you were talking about sugar.

That is all right; I am talking about primary producers now. They had 

364 sows in those parishes a year ago. They took a survey the other day and they had only 34 sows left. If you can tell me how we can get pork by acting in that way I shall be happy. Right now the shelves in the dealers' stores are almost empty of bacon. They cannot get enough bacon to supply the ordinary trade. They are having great difficulty. It will not be very long until we will be importing corn-fed hogs from the United States to satisfy our domestic market. If you call that a good hog policy, I do not. I do not think we have had a hog policy at all. As I said before, if it was a policy to put the producer out of business it certainly succeeded.
There are a few other things I wanted to say, but I do not think there is any necessity for me to carry on. I may tell the Minister of Agriculture something else. He was supposed to have put a floor under beef. He put a floor under beef at 26 cents.
What is the debate on, anyway?

Order. I did not want to interrupt the hon. member. A moment ago he was talking about hogs. I must tell him that he must speak to the subject under discussion, because if he changes the subject, then some other hon. member might be prevented from discussing the sugar beet industry, which is the subject being discussed.
What about the hon. member for Charlotte?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: What he said related to the sugar beet agreements that were referred to by the hon. member who first introduced the subject. That is all the hon. member for Charlotte discussed. As long as the hon. member for Huron North was discussing the situation of the primary producer with reference to the sugar beet industry and related other matters, he was quite in order. I should like to suggest to him that if he gets further away from the subject he may find himself out of order.

If Your Honour decides that I cannot talk about the primary producer in any other industry than sugar beets, then I shall quit. I should like to tell the Minister of Agriculture just what effect his 26-cent floor under beef has had.
Do that on my estimates. Let us get into supply.

In the first place we lost 10 cents a pound directly on the beef. I asked the minister a question in the house one day as to what the floor constituted; was it on red brand beef or what was it on. He

said it was on a good steer, but a good steer would vary three or four cents a pound for that matter. But that is not what I started out to tell him. His floor under beef actually turned out to be a ceiling for the packers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. For the
information of hon. members generally who may take part in the debate perhaps I should quote citation 345, which has reference to the debate that may take place on the motion to go into supply. It is the citation which says that a subject once introduced is the one that has to be debated until that matter is disposed of. If any hon. member introduces a new subject, them others who follow are prevented from discussing the one that was originally introduced. The last four or five lines of the citation read:
Members may discuss various matters on the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair without any amendment being proposed; but once debate is stopped on one matter and another matter intervenes, members cannot again discuss the former.
Of course the hon. member for Huron North-and perhaps others-will say that he was discussing the former matter. I suppose he will have to submit himself to my interpretation and agree that the subject that was introduced was not the whole agricultural policy of the government, but the beet sugar situation at the moment. The hon. member may now continue.

All right; I will not refer to the Minister of Agriculture's floor on beef any more, because it was not a floor anyway. I should like to quote a few figures to show the money paid out annually to the farmers for sugar beets. It amounts to $5,500,000 a year.
That is in Ontario.

Yes, and almost an equal amount for labour, material and supplies. The sugar beet industry is worth at least $11 million a year to the people of Ontario. Annually the farmers buy $220,000 worth of fertilizers and $100,000 worth of sugar beet machinery. If these men are put out of business all that machinery will be useless for anything else on those farms. It is entirely different from any other kind of farm equipment. Then, 32,000 acres of sugar beets are grown in Ontario each year. We have here an industry that has no worries from the standpoint of competition because, no matter how much they produce, we can absorb it.
It will be recalled by hon. members that during the war years sugar was rationed. If it had not been for the fact that we had some sugar refineries in Canada we would have
Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement had no sugar at all, because our supplies went to the bottom of the ocean. We were rationed because we had not sufficient in this country to go around. That condition could come again, and very soon, if this shooting war should ever develop. We know it could develop, and if it did we would be in the same position we were before. Our sugar industry would be lost, and we would have no sugar whatsoever.
For that reason I claim something should be done for the industry, if it is at all possible, to keep these sugar beet growers in business. They do not affect any other industry in this country; they are doing a good job for Canada, and we need their sugar.

Mr. Speaker, I feel I should make a few remarks in connection with the sugar beet situation, because the subject was introduced tonight by my good friend from Lambton West (Mr. Murphy). He made reference to the fact that while in Sarnia I had made some comments about sugar. I went up there the other night to make it a little easier for him politically, and I did make a brief reference to sugar.
The newspapers do not always quote one correctly, because I did not have notes to hand to the press. I was speaking more or less off the cuff, because I have always felt that I know something about sugar beets and the problems of sugar beet growers in this country. However, I feel more or less an amateur here tonight in listening to so many professionals who have spoken on the subject.
I did say in Sarnia that I was sure this government did not want to put any primary industry out of business. I said I was sure that the government did not want to see the sugar beet industry in Ontario thrown to the wolves. My good friend from Lambton West has said that I had said they were being thrown to the wolves. Well, I did not say that at all. The hon. member said in his speech that the sugar beet growers had been sold down the river; and when he refers to being sold down the river I assume he means through the trade agreement that was made with Cuba. I have said before and I say again-

On a point of order, I am sure the hon. member would not want to leave a wrong impression on Hansard. I did not say they were sold down the river because of the agreement. I think I emphasized that it was because of the importation of refined sugar that they were being sold down the river.

I would have to read the speech again to be sure, and I want to be

Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement fair to the hon. member. However, I understood him to say that the agreement we had made with Cuba, whereby we take raw sugar, was the cause of our difficulty, through getting refined sugar. If I am wrong, then I am sorry.
The hon. member also made reference to the fact that at the conference which was held here last October between the growers, the refiners and officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Finance, the question of dumping was not discussed. He said that dumping was never mentioned at all. Well, the question of dumping was mentioned. No one said they were dumping sugar. All I said in Sarnia, and all I had said previously, was that the dumping duty is a potential protection, and that is all a dumping duty is for at any time. In some cases, if an article is selling in this country at a reasonable price and is not underselling the home market product, it is of course difficult to apply a dumping duty.
Again, reference has been made by the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Cardiff) -who I am sure is as interested as I am in the sugar beet industry-to the fact that the government paid out of the consolidated revenue fund enough money to make up the difference between the cost of Cuban sugar, with duty, so that it would be the same as British empire sugar. Well, the fact of the matter is that British empire raw sugar or, to be more exact, United Kingdom sugar, comes in at a rate of approximately 29 or 30 cents a hundredweight. The duty on raw sugar coming in from Cuba is approximately $1 more per hundredweight. The British government, or British traders, are pretty shrewd dealers, and they take advantage of that extra protection from Cuba. The result is that they absorb 85 cents out of every dollar in the price of sugar bought from empire countries.
So what happens in connection with bringing in Cuban raw sugar is that the refiners bring the raw sugar in and pay $1 per hundredweight extra duty into the consolidated revenue fund, and the government has only to pay about 15 cents in order to have it cost the same as British empire sugar. So actually it does not cost the consolidated revenue fund anything. As a matter of fact a question in this connection was asked on the order paper, and the answer indicated that under the three-year agreement there was almost $6 million in revenue that had accrued as a result of this Cuban agreement.
World prices of raw sugar have dropped. On December 12 I said that from 1951 the price of raw sugar had dropped by approximately $1.85 a hundredweight. According to
[Mr. MacKenzie.l

deliveries now being offered from Cuba, that quotation has now dropped another 70 cents a hundredweight. So that actually there has been a drop from 1951 to the present time in the world price of raw sugar-and I do not care whether it is British empire or Cuban sugar-of almost $2.50 a hundredweight. So it is pretty difficult to know just what the answer is in regard to the importation of refined sugar.
Let me say that I did not say at any time, as some hon. members have said, that 2 per cent was only a trivial thing. I never said that at all. On December 12 I did say that it was a trifle over 2 per cent of our annual consumption and that, in itself, I said was not disastrous. I pointed out, however, that if it continued it could lead to a great deal of trouble. However, I never said it was a trifling thing or a small thing at any time. It means a lot to bring that much sugar into any area that produces sugar, and has always had the home market. I am not too sure that if importations of refined sugar from Cuba are stopped you are going to eliminate completely importations of refined sugar from the Philippines, from Santo Domingo and from Haiti. I am not sure about that, because refined sugar costs must be lower in those countries. I should like to have the figures on that in order to be sure.
There was one thing I was rather amazed at tonight when the hon. member for Lamb-ton West (Mr. Murphy) brought this up. He mentioned that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) had made a statement to the press. When the delegation met him in October the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that he would be making a trip to South America and would make a point of going to Cuba early in February to discuss with trade officials there the sugar agreement and the whole Cuban treaty, and see if some amicable agreement could not be reached.
On January 20 the hon. member for Lamb-ton West made his speech in St. Thomas. He dealt with sugar beets, and he advertised that pretty extensively. I was pleased to note that in some of the advertisements he said to come early to get a seat, as there would be no admission. I was glad of that because I was sure that would be a good inducement.
In his speech the hon. member suggested to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that he make a trip to Cuba to discuss with the trade officials this very agreement we are discussing tonight. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has not been in his place here to make a statement. Why should we

Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement
not wait until he gets back before saying anything further on the sugar beet industry? After all, all we have is a press statement. We have nothing direct from him. Why not wait until he comes back, when he will probably have a statement to make regarding the Cuban situation and the Cuban treaty, regarding refined and raw sugar.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The press statement was made two days before the meeting with the Cuban authorities.

Knowing that the minister will be here tomorrow or the next day and be prepared to make his statement, why not wait until he makes that statement before we condemn the policy as a whole?
I was quite interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart). The sugar beet industry has played a most important part in the economy of this country. When you run into a condition where you have depressed selling of sugar, where there is a surplus of that commodity, I do not think it is fair that one industry should bear the brunt of that situation. I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce understands that quite well, and I feel satisfied that we will reach a solution of this in the near future.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know that I agree entirely with the previous speaker that we should necessarily wait for the return of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I say this because the sugar beet industry in Canada has more ramifications to it than could be covered in an interview by the minister with Cuban authorities in respect of the importation of Cuban sugar. Because the sugar beet industry of Canada has those many ramifications I think it appropriate that we should discuss it at this time.
I have many notes here and I cannot conclude what I have to say in three minutes, so may I ask you to call it ten o'clock.
Go on.

No.

speechtext: -that I call it ten o'clock?
No.
Agreed.
All right; I can fiddle around here for three minutes.
How do you spell that?
It is obvious to me that hon. members opposite would like to close the debate on this particular subject.
Why should you close it?

I was not going to close it. We still live in a free country and we still operate in a free parliament, we hope. Members are sent down here to represent their constituents and to voice their grievances. It happens that some of us live in areas where they grow sugar beets and refine sugar. Because we believe that industry has a grievance, we are going to debate that matter here.
On motion of Mr. Hansell the debate was adjourned.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with regard to the business for tomorrow I do not think I need repeat what I said last night; it will be the same program tomorrow as we had today.

When is the government going to afford the house an opportunity to resume consideration of the motion to set up the special committee on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? It is two weeks since that was up for discussion, and the committee should be working now. The days are slipping by.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No one is more anxious than I to see that debate resumed, but we cannot have two debates going on in the house at the same time. What am I to say to these hon. members?
The minister had a quite different excuse when I asked about this two weeks ago. He said there was another debate that was going to take one day.
